inline.s: All people delight in fortune and dread misfortune. Hence to win fortune and avert calamity is the common wish of humankind. But often things run counter to one's wishes: one seeks fortune and fortune slips away; one would avert calamity and calamity comes. Why is this? Tracing the causes, there are several kinds:
First, some do not know and do not believe that “doing good brings fortune, and abandoning evil averts calamity.”
Second, some know and believe that “doing good brings fortune, and abandoning evil averts calamity,” yet do not know concretely how to put it into practice.

Third, some know and believe that “doing good brings fortune, and abandoning evil averts calamity,” and also know concretely how to practice it, but they are short-sighted and weak-willed, unable to resist the lure of desire, licking honey from the blade's edge and drinking poison to quench their thirst.

Fourth, the retributive justice of cause and effect reaches across the three times, and moreover its retributions include hidden retribution, unseen retribution, and retribution that lightens a heavy offense. Ordinary eyes cannot see the cause and effect of the three times, nor the strength of past karma, whether good or evil. Seeing that many who cultivate virtue or commit evil show no obvious retribution, they come to doubt the justice of cause and effect.

[The three times] The past, the present, and the future. [The retributive justice of cause and effect reaches across the three times] Retribution is of three kinds: immediate retribution, retribution in the next life, and retribution in a later life. Immediate retribution is when one does good or evil in this life and reaps good or evil reward in this very life. Retribution in the next life is when one receives the retribution in the life to come. Retribution in a later life is when one finally receives retribution after two, three, a hundred, or a thousand lives. The Buddha said: If you wish to know the causes of your past life, look at what you receive in this life; if you wish to know the fruits of your future life, look at what you do in this life.

The Illustrated Compendium on the Ganying Pian records: In the Ming dynasty, in Yangzhou, there was a wealthy man who traded goods between north and south (buying and selling goods from one region to another to earn the price difference). He had a son of noble character and two grandsons of outstanding intelligence. As he lay dying, the wealthy man secretly handed a steelyard to his son and said, “This is the treasure that built our household; guard it well!” The son asked, “Why is it the family treasure?” The rich man said, “This steelyard is made of ebony, and it conceals mercury inside. When selling, I pour mercury into the head, so people think it weighs more, not knowing it actually weighs less; when buying, I pour mercury into the tail, so people think it is light, not knowing it is actually heavy. Thus I grew rich!” The son was shocked inwardly but dared not speak. After his father died and the funeral was finished, he prayed to Heaven, begging forgiveness for his father's offenses, and burned the steelyard. In the smoke something rose aloft like a green snake. Not long afterward, his two sons both died one after another. He sighed, “Heaven has no awareness; cause and effect are reversed.” Day after day he was dazed and weary, no longer wishing to live. One day he dreamed that a god in golden armor instructed him, “Your father, because of the manifold minor good deeds of his past life, was destined to be wealthy; it had nothing to do with the steelyard. Because in this life his heart was unjust, the Jade Emperor sent the two stars of Ruin and Exhaustion to bring down his household, and after the household fell, to follow with fire. Now, because you have washed away your father's offenses, the two stars of Ruin and Exhaustion are withdrawn, and a worthy son will bring glory to your house. You should earnestly practice good deeds and not harbor resentment.” He woke and understood, and his resolve to do good grew firmer. In the end two sons were born, and both passed the imperial examination.

Comment: Just this one case can prove that cause and effect reach across the three times without error. See how the god in golden armor said to the worthy son, “Your father, because of the manifold minor good deeds of his past life, was destined to be wealthy; it had nothing to do with the steelyard.” This proves the later-life retribution of good done in a former life. And because the rich man's heart was unjust in this life, the two stars of Ruin and Exhaustion were sent to bring down his household, and after it fell, fire followed; this proves the immediate retribution of evil done in this life. And because the worthy son could wash away his father's faults and act fairly, the two stars were especially withdrawn so that the worthy son would bring glory to the family; this proves the immediate retribution of good done in this life. Later-life and immediate retribution being thus, retribution in the next life can be inferred as well. The rich man spent his life deceiving people with the steelyard and causing them to suffer loss; that was great evil, so the Jade Emperor sent the two stars to bring down his household, to show how swift is immediate retribution. The worthy son burned the steelyard and secretly prayed to Heaven, begging forgiveness for his father's sins; that was great good, so the Jade Emperor withdrew the two stars so that the worthy son would illuminate the family after him. Is this not enjoying the bliss of immediate retribution? Thus one can also understand that the principles of good fortune and ill fortune, of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, support and conceal each other in turn, only they are not what ordinary eyes can see.
The Ganying Pian lucidly sets forth the principles of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, of fortune and misfortune, and lists more than
good deeds and more than

evil deeds, concretely and comprehensively explaining the content of good and evil. The principles are clear and the practices are concrete, sincere and genuine. To revere and uphold it, and to practice according to it, will surely bring fortune and avert calamity.

The Illustrated Compendium on the Ganying Pian says: “The Ganying Pian is the numinous text that rescues from suffering, the wondrous truth that averts calamity. If a person reveres and upholds it, then at all times and in all places auspicious spirits will protect him, and all evil stars will retreat far away; naturally, meeting difficulty one finds safety, and encountering misfortune one turns it to good.”

Emperor Wenchang said: “I now exhort the people of the world to recite the Taishang Ganying Pian once each day, and to practice according to it; and to copy out one volume (that is, write out one copy), gazing upon it morning and evening, and practice in accordance with it.”

The Compilation on the Taishang Ganying Pian says: “One who upholds this text must continually recite it silently in the heart, and let each word reflect back upon oneself: Do I have such a matter? And so, gradually, it diminishes. Every day thus, every year thus, then naturally wherever one acts is good, and wherever one touches is good.”

Master Yinguang said: “The Taishang Ganying Pian gathers the supreme principles of favoring the auspicious, opposing the inauspicious, blessing good, and punishing licentiousness, and sets them forth in arguments that shake heaven and move earth and startle the eye and the heart. What is good? What is evil? What good reward does one who does good receive? What evil reward does one who does evil receive? It sees into the very roots, clear as watching a person. Moreover, fools who are unwilling to do good and willfully do evil act so because the mind of selfish gain drives them. Now, knowing that the selfish are instead losing great benefit and incurring great calamity, who would not strive earnestly toward goodness, hoping to extinguish calamity and gather fortune? From this we can say that this book benefits people deeply! Hence the great Confucian scholars of old mostly relied on it for their quiet cultivation.” “Taking this book to its ultimate conclusion, it merely reaches becoming an immortal;

if one practices it with the great bodhi resolve, then one can transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, put an end to birth and death, sever the three delusions to realize the Dharmakaya, and perfect blessing and wisdom to accomplish the Buddha path; how much less the small fruit of becoming an immortal, merely a human or heavenly reward!
” (From the Preface to the Direct Lectures on the Taishang Ganying Pian)

[Favoring the auspicious] “Favored” means giving people wealth or benefits. Here “auspicious” means good, virtuous, and admirable. For example, “the good man is aided by Heaven.” [A good man is helped by Heaven] A good man will receive Heaven's help. “Help” means assistance and protection. [Punishing licentiousness] “Punish” means to bring calamity upon. Here “licentiousness” means evil. [The three delusions] The delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of dust and sand, and the delusion of fundamental ignorance. The delusion of views and thoughts is the delusion of ordinary beings. In it, the delusion of views is confusion and error in knowledge and views, such as the five wrong views of self-view and extreme views; the delusion of thoughts is confusion and error in thought, such as the five afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. If practitioners of the Sravaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles sever these two delusions, they can realize the arhat fruit and escape the three realms. The delusion of dust and sand is the delusion of bodhisattvas: if bodhisattvas, in delivering and transforming sentient beings, do not understand the countless Dharma doors, as numerous as dust and sand, they cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings; hence it is called the delusion of dust and sand. The delusion of fundamental ignorance is the fundamental ignorance that obscures the principle of the middle-way true reality; when it is completely severed, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, the delusion of views and thoughts is coarse, the delusion of dust and sand is middling, and the delusion of fundamental ignorance is subtle.

In the Ming dynasty, Minister of Justice Liu (the Minister of Punishments) was kind-hearted and forbearing, upheld the law with fairness, and was never harsh. His son Liu Jing was extremely frail and often ill. Above him he had five elder brothers, all of whom had died young. The Minister of Justice, seeing that his only remaining sixth son was so sickly, was deeply worried. Whenever he met a fortune-teller or physiognomist, he would ask them to calculate Liu Jing's fortune. But unfortunately, most of the astrologers said that Liu Jing would face a great calamity at the age of nineteen, and this made his father worry all the more. Just then, a physiognomist from Sichuan, Zhou Shilian, came to the capital to practice divination by reading faces; his readings were extremely accurate, and his fame shook the whole capital inside and out. So Minister of Justice Liu invited Zhou Shilian to his home and asked him to examine Liu Jing's lifelong fortune, rank, and longevity.
[Emolument] The salary of officials in ancient times; also used figuratively for wealth and honor.

Zhou the physiognomist looked for a long while, then said, “As for the young gentleman's lifespan, I fear he may not pass the threshold of nineteen. But you must not be discouraged because of this. You must know that ‘destiny is appointed by Heaven, but the establishment of one's life is in oneself.’ By and large, whether a person's emolument and longevity are thick or thin relates to the good or evil of the karmic causes created in former lives. The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha's Primal Vows says that one who killed living beings in former lives must suffer the retribution of a short life in this life. If this is so, then the young gentleman's karma of killing in his former life must be very heavy. Since we already know the cause of his short-lived appearance, there is a remedy. By abstaining from killing and releasing living beings, and broadly cultivating all kinds of good karma to make up for it, it is not difficult to change a short life into a long one. It is like a sick person whose illness has been diagnosed; one need only prescribe the right medicine and he will in time recover. But as for cultivating goodness, one must do so with utmost effort. One must achieve that the good karma of this life far outweighs the evil karma of past lives before one can see real results. Suppose the young gentleman's past evil karma is eight parts; if in this life he repents of evil and cultivates good, he must achieve a full ten parts in order to add back and make up for the emolument and longevity fixed by his physiognomy. If he only attains six or seven parts, or barely the eight, then good will not overcome evil; this is like a serious illness with a weak medicine that is hard to revive the dying, and it may be hard to see immediate results. But this does not mean that doing good comes to nothing; these good deeds are still useful in planting good roots for future lives. The world often sees many who cultivate virtue or commit evil with no obvious retribution, and so they doubt that Heaven is unaware. That is because with the fleshly eye they cannot see the cause and effect of the three times, nor the strength of their past karma. I earnestly hope you father and son will deeply believe the Buddha's words, which are true and not false. Do it with all sincerity, and the young gentleman will surely enjoy long fortune and longevity; there is no need to worry.” Then he taught them to uphold the Taishang Ganying Pian and to practice it without cease.

At this time Liu Jing was only seventeen, intelligent and much given to self-exhortation. Hearing Zhou the physiognomist's words, he regarded them as the words of utmost truth, so he made a vow before Heaven, resolving to uphold the Taishang Ganying Pian, to abandon evil and cultivate goodness. He copied out the clauses of good and evil in the Ganying Pian one by one. The good ones he posted on the east wall; each time he did one good deed he added a red circle. The evil ones he posted on the west wall; each time he committed one evil he added a black circle. Even when a thought stirred, he rigorously reproved himself and dared not indulge himself. As for abstaining from killing and releasing living beings, he practiced it with especial effort and was never lax. In this way he kept on for three years and safely passed the barrier at nineteen.

One day, on business he took a boat across the Yangtze and saw a fisherman net a very large turtle. Liu Jing, touched by compassion, ordered his attendants to give a thousand coins to buy it and release it. Strangely enough, the turtle, once in the water, seemed to have intelligence: it raised its head and nodded, then followed behind Liu Jing's boat to escort him. It accompanied him for five li, and when Liu Jing went ashore it was still reluctant to leave. That night Liu Jing, in the inn, dreamed of a black-clad, short, stout Taoist who said to him, “You, young sir, have practiced the Ganying Pian for three years without weariness, and the Heavenly Emperor greatly commends you; you have now been granted increased emolument and extended longevity. But your constitution is weak, and it is hard to guarantee that you will not be harmed by cold and heat. I have a small technique to teach you; by relying on it to regulate your body you may keep safe and free of illness.” Having said this, he passed on a method of regulating the breath to remove illness.

When Liu Jing woke, he knew the divine turtle had repaid his virtue. From then on, practicing according to the method, he grew healthier day by day. Later, Minister of Justice Liu again invited Zhou Shilian to his home to thank him for his former guidance. That night Zhou Shilian and Liu Jing slept in the same bed. Waking at midnight, Zhou saw Liu Jing sound asleep with not the slightest breath; when he felt him, he was like a dead man. The next morning he went and congratulated Minister Liu, saying, “It has been several years and the young gentleman's bone structure differs greatly from before. Watching him as he sleeps, he has clearly received the instruction of the turtle-breath. Not only is his health good and his life long, but his future fortune will stretch on without limit. This is exactly the retribution of your father and son's sincere practice of good!” In the end Liu Jing lived to ninety-eight, with worthy and talented descendants, complete blessing and longevity; and indeed Zhou Shilian's prophecy was fulfilled.
Q: What is the significance of studying the Ganying Pian for one who studies Buddhism?
A: It is of very great significance. The core of the Ganying Pian is: follow the principle of Heaven and remove selfish desire. In the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha said:
“You bhikshus, being already able to abide in the precepts, should restrain the five faculties and not let them be unrestrained and enter the five desires.”
In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections, the Buddha said:
“One who practices the Way is like a person wrapped in dry grass
(like one whose body is wrapped in dry grass)
: when fire comes, one must flee. A person of the Way, seeing desire, must always distance himself from it.”

Therefore, believing in cause and effect, following the principle of Heaven, and removing selfish desire are the foundation of studying Buddhism. Hence Master Yinguang spared no effort in promoting the Ganying Pian, as can be seen throughout his Collected Writings. Master Yinguang said:

“The Taishang Ganying Pian gathers the supreme principles of favoring the auspicious, opposing the inauspicious, blessing good, and punishing licentiousness, and sets them forth in arguments that shake heaven and move earth and startle the eye and heart. What is good? What is evil? What good reward does one who does good receive? What evil reward does one who does evil receive? It sees into the very roots, clear as watching a person.” “Taking this book to its ultimate conclusion, it merely reaches becoming an immortal; if one practices it with the great bodhi resolve, then one can transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, put an end to birth and death, sever the three delusions to realize the Dharmakaya, and perfect blessing and wisdom to accomplish the Buddha path; how much less the small fruit of becoming an immortal, merely a human or heavenly reward!”
(From the Preface to the Direct Lectures on the Taishang Ganying Pian)

[The five faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. [The five desires] The desires for forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles. Forms mean beautiful appearances; sounds mean pleasing voices and charming speech; scents mean fragrant odors; tastes mean delicious flavors; tangibles means agreeable bodily contact. Because these five can give rise to the mind of greed and desire, they are called the five desires. To be pure in the precepts is to be able to control the five faculties and not be moved by the five desires.
For the Pure Land practitioner, in the Amitābha Sutra the Buddha said:
“One cannot be born in that land with few good roots, blessings, and karmic conditions.”

In the three provisions for the Pure Land, of faith, vow, and practice, the vow is: to detach from the Saha world and aspire with joy to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. And it is required that one's right mindfulness be clear and distinct at death
(with the ten thoughts continuous at the moment of death; see
The Conditions for Rebirth

. Just consider: if selfish desire is always in control, where can the good roots, blessings, and virtues be spoken of? Where can detachment from the Saha world be spoken of? And at death, can one's right mindfulness be clear and distinct
(with the ten thoughts continuous)
[Good roots] That is, the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because they can produce wondrous fruits, they are called good roots.

For the Chan practitioner, one must achieve no-self and no-thought. If selfish desire is always in control, can one achieve no-self and no-thought? One will surely be mouthing emptiness while every step grasps at existence.
So Master Yinguang said:
“The Dharma of cause and effect is the great furnace
(in the mundane and supramundane worlds)

by which all sages smelt the ordinary and refine the sage. If from the very start one does not investigate cause and effect, then after having penetrated the tenets and the teachings, one may still commit errors in the matter of cause and effect. Once cause and effect go wrong, there is the prospect of falling, and no way of ascending. And do not slight this principle as shallow and near-at-hand and thus neglect it. When the Tathagata attains right enlightenment and sentient beings fall into the three evil paths, none of it goes beyond cause and effect. Because the mind of the ordinary person is small, where the scriptures speak of great cause and effect one may not fully grasp it; one should use the shallow and near-at-hand in the world as a convenient means of entering what is superior. Such as the Wenchang Yinzhi Wen
(namely the Emperor Wenchang's Tract on Hidden Virtue)
and the Taishang Ganying Pian, etc., causing
(make)
one to read them thoroughly and practice them with careful examination; then everyone can become a good person, and everyone can put an end to birth and death.”
(From his Reply to Layman Xie Chengming of Sichuan) Pay special attention to this sentence, “everyone can put an end to birth and death.”
[The mundane and supramundane worlds] The mundane world and the supramundane world. The mundane world is the world of sentient beings; the supramundane world is the world of Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
[Hidden virtue (yin-zhi, pronounced
zh

Q: Above it says “remove selfish desire”; is this not asceticism?
A: First, we must understand the principle of why we should remove selfish desire. Confucius said:
“What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others.”

(Translation: What one is unwilling to accept for oneself cannot be imposed upon others.) Why must we impose nothing on others that we do not wish for ourselves? Besides the moral, conscientious, and even legal requirements that we should do so, there is a still deeper reason: “Whatever you send out, it all comes back to you.” This is the law of the universe. Like the law of action and reaction in physics, so long as there is an action, there must be a reaction; push the wall, and the wall pushes you. Whatever you send out, you will receive. Do evil, and evil will be imposed upon you; speak evil, and evil words will be imposed upon you; harbor evil intent, and evil intent will be imposed upon you. Conversely, do good, and good will be imposed upon you; speak good, and good words will be imposed upon you; harbor good intent, and good intent will be imposed upon you. This is the law of the universe!

There is a saying, “Please get into the jar,” which tells the story of Zhou Xing, a cruel official under Empress Wu. Someone secretly reported that Zhou Xing had colluded with Qiu Shenji to rebel, so Empress Wu ordered Lai Junchen to try the case. So Lai Junchen invited Zhou Xing home as a guest, and while making merry over wine, they discussed various cases. Lai Junchen said to Zhou Xing, “Some prisoners repeatedly interrogated still refuse to confess their crimes; is there any way to make them confess?” Zhou Xing said, “This is easy! Just take a jar, heat it all around with charcoal fire, then put the prisoner inside; what crime would he dare not to confess?” Lai Junchen then ordered his attendants to find a jar and heat it around with charcoal in the manner Zhou Xing described, then stood up and said to Zhou Xing, “Someone has reported you for rebellion; the Empress has ordered me to examine you. I beg you, elder brother, to get into this jar yourself (the phrase ‘please get into the jar’)!” Zhou Xing was greatly alarmed and immediately kowtowed and confessed.
The great judge of the universe is likewise: for all who do evil, he will please get them into the jar. Hence, in the Buddha Treasury Sutra the Buddha said:
“Evil begets evil retribution.”

That is, there being an evil cause, there must be an evil fruit. The wise fear the cause, knowing that creating a cause must bring a fruit; the foolish fear the fruit, because they do not believe in the law of cause and effect, or are unwilling to believe in it, and so act without restraint when creating causes. When calamity comes, they are thrown into panic, cursing Heaven and blaming others, only never knowing to blame themselves.

Whatever you send out, it all comes back to you” — this law of the universe likewise applies to those of good heart, good speech, and good conduct. So after the Buddha said “evil begets evil retribution,” he immediately went on to say:
“Good begets good retribution.”
“Evil begets evil retribution, good begets good retribution” — this is the law of causal retribution of the universe, or what is called retributive justice.

People of the world are all “short-sighted,” seeing only the present, not knowing there is a future, much less a life to come. It is like the cicada that only enjoys the summer, not knowing that autumn and winter will follow in turn!
There is a famous saying in philosophy:
Freedom is the recognition of necessity.

Most people suppose freedom means doing whatever one pleases; they forget that this “doing whatever one pleases” is creating a cause, and that a fruit will surely come to requite it. You have the freedom to jump from a building, and you also have the freedom to break your legs; you have the freedom to eat and drink to excess, and you also have the freedom to be afflicted with illness. Such a cause, such a fruit. Hence the wise know that only by deeply recognizing necessity (causal retribution) can one attain true freedom. If you want the fruit of winning fortune and averting calamity, you must create the cause of winning fortune and averting calamity. If you want the fruit of health, happiness, and longevity, you must create the cause of health, happiness, and longevity.

The above speaks of the mundane Dharma. The goal of a Buddhist is transcendence, to depart the three realms and put an end to birth and death. The Pure Land practitioner of Buddha-recitation must achieve right mindfulness clear and distinct at death (with the ten thoughts continuous); the Chan practitioner must gather the ten thousand thoughts into one, and the one into nothing, so as to see the nature and attain enlightenment. Therefore, besides cultivating concentration, one must also pare away the entangling force of the mundane world. The mind is like a horse: if it is a tamed horse, a touch of the reins will keep it from straying, and it will even know by itself to walk the right path. If it is an untamed horse, you must tighten the reins (concentration) at all times and places to govern it. Once its wildness erupts, you may not be able to control it! Removing selfish desire is just to pare away the entangling force of the mundane world, so that one's cultivation gains power, right mindfulness is clear and distinct at death, and one assures the end of birth and death and departure from the three realms.
Having read these words, will you still regard removing selfish desire as folly, as superstition, as so-called “asceticism”?

inline.s: (From the old block imprint: dictated by Emperor Wenchang)

Emperor Wenchang said: “For seventeen lives I have been a scholar-official, and never have I mistreated the people or been cruel to my subordinates. I relieved people's urgency and aided their want; I tolerated people's faults and pitied their loneliness. With a single mind thus, and obedient to Heaven, therefore I was able for a long time to realize the true position.”

Emperor Wenchang said: For seventeen lives I have been a scholar-official and never mistreated the people or treated my subordinates cruelly. I relieved people's urgent difficulties and helped in their want; I tolerated people's faults and pitied their loneliness. With a single mind thus, diligently advancing without slack, obedient to Heaven's ordering, and practicing for a long time, therefore I was able to realize the position of the True Lord.

[Emperor Wenchang] Also called “Emperor Wenchang” or “Lord Wenchang.” Emperor Wenchang is the god honored by the people and by Daoism as presiding over the fame, rank, and emolument of scholars. “Wenchang” was originally the name of a constellation, also called the Wenchang star or the literary star, the constellation that presides over the fortune of literature and fame.
[The True Lord]
Daoism calls those who attain the Way and become immortals true persons, and among them the highest in rank are called true lords.

“Now I exhort the people of the world to recite the Taishang Ganying Pian once each day and to practice in accordance with it; and to write out one volume, gazing upon it morning and evening, and practice accordingly. Practice it for two years, and ten thousand offenses are extinguished; practice it for four years, and all blessings gather; practice it for seven years, and descendants are worthy and intelligent, ascending to honor in the examinations; practice it for ten years, and life is lengthened; practice it for fifteen years, and all things go as one wishes; practice it for twenty years, and descendants become ministers and chancellors; practice it for thirty years, and a name is entered in the register of immortals
(the same as “immortal”)
; practice it for fifty years, and the gods of heaven bow in reverence, and the name is ranked among the immortal host.”

Now I exhort the people of the world: recite the Taishang Ganying Pian once each day and practice in accordance with it; and write out one copy, gazing upon it reverently morning and evening, and practice accordingly. Practice it for two years, and ten thousand offenses are extinguished; practice it for four years, and a hundred blessings gather; practice it for seven years, and descendants are worthy and intelligent, ascending to honor in the examinations (gloriously passing as scholars); practice it for ten years, and life is lengthened; practice it for fifteen years, and all things go as one wishes; practice it for twenty years, and descendants become ministers and chancellors; practice it for thirty years, and a name is recorded in the register of immortals; practice it for fifty years, and the gods of heaven bow in reverence, and one attains immortality.
[A volume (zhi, pronounced
zh
)] A measure word, used for a bound set of thread-bound books.
One volume: one book, one set. [Ascend to honor in the examinations] Gloriously
pass the examinations as a scholar.

“If one does not earnestly practice in accordance with this, doing sometimes and stopping sometimes, practicing today and abandoning tomorrow; then, since one's dealings with people have gone awry, the field of the heart grows dark day by day; though one recites the scripture, the mind does not awaken. This is to profane Heaven, an offense not to be forgiven.”

If one does not earnestly practice according to the instructions of the Taishang Ganying Pian, doing sometimes and stopping sometimes, practicing today and discarding tomorrow; then in dealing with people and affairs, one violates the principles and the listed practices that the Ganying Pian sets forth (in dealings with people, going against them); the field of the heart grows dark day by day; though one recites the scripture (the Taishang Ganying Pian) aloud, the mind does not awaken. This is to profane Heaven, an offense not to be forgiven.
[Cease (chuo, pronounced
chu
To stop.

blocks.text: The Original Text of the Ganying Pian

inline.s: The Exalted One said: “Fortune and misfortune have no door; they are summoned by a person alone. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow and its form.”

Therefore Heaven and Earth have spirits that oversee transgressions, and according to the gravity of a person's offenses they take away his reckoning. When the reckoning is diminished, one becomes poor and worn, meets with many sorrows and calamities, all people detest him, punishments and misfortunes follow him, auspicious celebrations shun him, and evil stars bring disaster upon him; when the reckoning is exhausted, he dies.

Moreover, there are the divine lords of the Three Terraces and the Big Dipper, dwelling above a person's head, recording his evil deeds and taking away his period and reckoning. There are also the Three Corpse Spirits, within a person's body, who on every Keng-shen day ascend to the heavenly offices and report a person's offenses. On the last day of the month, the Kitchen God does likewise. Whatever offense a person has, if great it takes away a period, if small it takes away a reckoning. These offenses, great and small, number several hundred; whoever wishes to seek long life must first guard against them.

What accords with the Way, advance toward; what does not accord with the Way, retreat from. Do not tread the path of evil; do not deceive in the dark chamber. Accumulate virtue and build up merit; have a compassionate heart toward all things. Be loyal, filial, friendly, and brotherly; rectify yourself and transform others. Pity the orphan and comfort the widow; revere the aged and cherish the young. Even insects and grass are not to be harmed. One should commiserate with others' misfortune and rejoice in others' good; relieve others' urgency and rescue others' peril; see others' gain as one's own gain; see others' loss as one's own loss. Do not publicize others' shortcomings; do not vaunt one's own strengths. Suppress evil and promote good; put aside the many and take the little. Bear insult without resentment; receive favor as if startled. Confer kindness without seeking return; give to others without regret.

As for the so-called good person, all people respect him, the Way of Heaven protects him, fortune and emolument follow him, all evil beings keep far from him, and spirits and sages guard him. Whatever he does is accomplished, and he may aspire to become an immortal. He who seeks to become a celestial immortal should establish thirteen hundred good deeds. He who seeks to become an earthly immortal should establish three hundred good deeds.

If one acts without righteousness and behaves contrary to principle; regards evil as ability and endures in cruelty and harm; secretly injures the good; covertly insults ruler and parents; slights one's teachers; betrays those one serves; deceives the ignorant; slanders fellow students; is false, vain, and fraudulent; attacks one's relatives; is stiff-necked and unkind; fierce and self-willed; judges right and wrong wrongly; turns toward and away inappropriately; oppresses subordinates to gain merit; flatters superiors to seek their favor; receives kindness without gratitude; and harbors resentment without end;

Despises the people of Heaven; disturbs the governance of the state; rewards the unrighteous; punishes the innocent; kills to take wealth; topples others to take position; executes the surrendered and slaughters the vanquished; demotes the upright and expels the worthy; bullies the orphan and oppresses the widow; abandons the law and takes bribes; regards the straight as crooked and the crooked as straight; treats the light as heavy; is the more enraged at seeing killing; knows fault yet does not reform; knows good yet does not do it; draws others into own guilt; obstructs the arts and methods; slanders sages and worthy ones; and violates virtue.

Shoots at flying birds and chases running beasts; disturbs hibernators and startles roosting birds; fills burrows and overturns nests; harms the embryo and breaks the egg; wishes others to suffer loss; destroys others' success; endangers others for one's own safety; diminishes others for one's own gain; exchanges what is evil for what is good; sets aside the public for the private; steals others' ability; conceals others' goodness; exposes others' ugliness; exposes others' private affairs; wastes others' wealth and goods; separates others from their flesh and blood; encroaches on others' loved ones; abets others in wrongdoing; displays one's might and is tyrannical; humiliates others to gain victory; ruins others' crops and harvests; breaks up others' marriages.

Grows proud upon wealth; is shameless upon escaping trouble; claims kindness and shifts blame; shifts calamity and sells evil; buys false reputation; harbors a treacherous heart; frustrates others' strengths; shields one's own faults; takes advantage of power to coerce; lets loose cruelty to wound and kill; cuts and tailors without cause; slaughters and cooks in violation of propriety; scatters and casts away the five grains; toils and disturbs the multitude; ruins others' households and takes their wealth; breaks dikes and sets fires to harm dwellings; confuses the rules and standards to ruin others' work; damages others' tools to make them useless.

Seeing others honored and noble, one wishes them exiled and disgraced; seeing others wealthy, one wishes them ruined and scattered; seeing others beautiful, one's heart stirs to covet them; owing others wealth and goods, one wishes their death; when requests are unfulfilled, one gives rise to curses and resentment; seeing others at a disadvantage, one speaks of their faults; seeing others' bodies imperfect, one laughs at them; seeing others' talents deserving praise, one suppresses them.

Buries charms to curse people; uses poisons to kill trees; is wrathful with teachers; is defiant toward father and elder brothers; demands forcibly and seeks forcibly; loves to encroach and seize; plunders to grow rich; is artfully deceitful to seek promotion; rewards and punishes unjustly; is licentious and revels beyond measure; is harsh and cruel to subordinates and intimidates others; curses Heaven and blames others; rails at the wind and berates the rain; foments quarrels and litigation; recklessly joins factions; heeds the words of wife and concubines and disobeys parents' teachings; forgets the old upon gaining the new; says one thing and means another; is greedy for wealth and deceives those above; makes evil speech to slander the innocent; slanders others and calls it upright; curses the gods and calls it correct; abandons the compliant and imitates the rebellious; turns from kin to strangers; points to Heaven and Earth to attest a base heart; invokes spirits and sages to witness obscene matters.

Repents of giving afterwards; borrows and fails to return; seeks what is beyond one's lot; schemes beyond one's strength; is excessive in lust; takes poison beyond measure; feeds others corrupted food; deludes the masses with heterodox ways; uses short measures and irregular cloth; uses light balance and small measures; mixes the false with the true; takes profit through craft; presses the good to be base; swindles the simple; is insatiably greedy; and curses and prays to demand righteousness.

Is given to wine and plays the rebel; kinfolk quarrel in anger; men are not loyal and good, women not gentle and obedient; does not harmonize with one's family; does not revere one's husband; always loves to boast and constantly practices envy; is without conduct toward wife and children; is discourteous to one's parents-in-law; slights the spirits of ancestors; disobeys the commands of superiors; does what is useless; harbors a divided heart; curses oneself and curses others; is partial in affection to one and aversion to another; steps over a well and over a stove; jumps over provisions and jumps over a person; harms one's children and aborts the unborn; practices much that is dark and hidden; feasts and sings on dark days and new moons; cries in anger on the first of the month; spits and urinates facing north; chants and weeps facing the stove; yet also burns incense at the stove fire; cooks with unclean wood; rises naked at night; executes punishments on the eight festivals; spits at meteors; points at the rainbow; points at the three lights by either daylight; gazes too long at sun and moon; hunts with fire in the spring month; curses bitterly facing north; without cause kills turtles and strikes snakes.

For such offenses as these, the Lord of Destiny takes away his period and reckoning according to their gravity. When the reckoning is exhausted, he dies. If there is blame remaining after death, it extends to plague his descendants.

Again: those who wrongfully seize the wealth of others — the reckoning is exacted from their wife, children, and household, until death and mourning come upon them. And if they do not die, then fire, flood, robbers, and thieves, the loss of their goods, illness, and quarrels and slander — all such things come upon them, to offset the value of what they wrongfully took.

Again: those who wrongfully kill others are but exchanging weapons to slay one another. Those who take wealth that is not rightfully theirs are like one who eats tainted meat to stay his hunger, or drinks poisoned wine to quench his thirst. It is not that he is not filled for a moment; death too comes upon him.

When the mind gives rise to good, though the good be not yet done, auspicious spirits already follow it. When the mind gives rise to evil, though the evil be not yet done, inauspicious spirits already follow it. But if one has done evil deeds and afterward repents and reforms, doing no evil and practicing every good, in the long run he will surely attain auspicious blessing. This is what is meant by turning calamity into fortune.

Therefore the auspicious person speaks good, looks upon good, and does good; with three goods in a single day, in three years Heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious person speaks evil, looks upon evil, and does evil; with three evils in a single day, in three years Heaven will surely send down calamity upon him. Why then will you not strive earnestly and put this into practice?

This text takes its name from the two words “ganying” — stimulus and response. The stimulus is the cause, the response is the fruit. “The fruit responds to the stimulus; where there is a cause, there must be a fruit” — this law of cause and effect governs the whole universe. Master Yinguang said: “Cause and effect is the great sovereign power by which the sages govern the world and the Buddhas deliver sentient beings. Speaking from the standpoint of the Buddhadharma, from the ground of the ordinary person all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood, not one dharma falls outside of cause and effect.” (From the preface to A Record of Root and Branch Together Cured, to Win Back the Hearts of the World, in the
Collected Writings of Master Yinguang)

The four lines at the beginning of this text — “Fortune and misfortune have no door; they are summoned by a person alone. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow and its form” — are the general outline of the whole work. They set forth that doing good (the cause) brings fortune (the fruit), and doing evil (the cause) brings misfortune (the fruit): this is the principle of karmic retribution. It is what is called the net of Heaven, wide and vast, which yet lets nothing slip through. In the Sutra of the Buddha Treasury the Buddha said: “Evil has its evil retribution, good has its good retribution.”

If a person understands the principle of cause and effect and knows that doing evil will surely bring calamity, then his mind will hold something in awe and he will not dare to do it; knowing that doing good will surely bring fortune and emolument, his mind will hold something it seeks and will not be willing to stop. Hence Master Yinguang said: “Cause and effect is the great sovereign power by which the sages govern the world and the Buddhas deliver sentient beings.” He also said: “The Taishang Ganying Pian gathers the supreme principles of favoring the auspicious, opposing the inauspicious, blessing the good, and punishing the licentious, and sets them forth in arguments that shake heaven and move earth and startle the eye and the heart. What is good? What is evil? What good reward does one who does good receive? What evil reward does one who does evil receive? It sees into the very roots, clear as watching a person.”

Therefore, in these present days, when the sea of desire runs wild and evil karma rages, it is of the utmost importance to vigorously promote education in cause and effect — this is the urgent task of the hour; and to lead by one's own example, since teaching by example is weightier than teaching by words, is important above all, for it is the precious raft that ferries others and oneself. Herein lies the meaning of practicing the Taishang Ganying Pian.

blocks.text: Chapter 1: The General Outline of the Whole Text

inline.s: [The Exalted One said: “Fortune and misfortune have no door; they are summoned by a person alone. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow and its form.”]

Lord Lao, the Exalted One, said: the descent of fortune and misfortune has no other cause — it is wholly summoned by one's own thoughts and actions. The retribution of good and evil in thought and action is like a shadow that follows the body and moves with it: doing evil one meets calamity, doing good one gains fortune.
[Lord Lao, the Exalted One]
The honorific title given by Daoism to Laozi; he is also called the Heavenly Worthy of the Way and Its Virtue.

All through a person's life he always wishes to avoid calamity and hasten toward fortune, yet things often run counter to his wishes. How, then, can one truly escape calamity and obtain fortune? The Taishang Ganying Pian is precisely concerned with this principle, and it goes further, teaching people concretely how to put it into practice, so as to attain the goal of escaping calamity and obtaining fortune.

Fortune and misfortune have no door; they are summoned by a person alone. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow and its form” — this single passage is the general outline of the whole text. It reveals the causal relation between fortune and misfortune on the one hand and evil and good on the other — the fruit responding to the stimulus (which is why it is called the “Ganying Pian,” the Text of Stimulus and Response). The descent of fortune and misfortune has no other cause; it is wholly summoned by one's own doing of evil or doing of good. Meeting calamity is because one has done evil; obtaining fortune is because one has done good. Plant melons and you get melons, plant beans and you get beans; such cause, such fruit, with not the slightest deviation. Whether it be fortune or misfortune, each person brings it upon himself (he makes the cause himself and receives the fruit himself). If a person constantly examines the two words “cause and effect” within himself, calamity will naturally be extinguished and fortune will arise.

The Taishang Ganying Pian sets out in detail: what is good and what is evil; how one must act to obtain fortune; how one must act to meet calamity. Walk according to it, and calamity will surely depart and fortune will surely come. Hence Emperor Wenchang said: “Now I exhort the people of the world to recite the Taishang Ganying Pian once each day, and to practice according to it; and to write out one volume, gazing upon it morning and evening, and practice in accordance with it. Practice it for two years, and ten thousand offenses are extinguished; practice it for four years, and a hundred blessings all gather; practice it for seven years, and descendants are worthy and intelligent, ascending to honor in the examinations; practice it for ten years, and life is lengthened; practice it for fifteen years, and all things go as one wishes; practice it for twenty years, and descendants become ministers and chancellors; practice it for thirty years, and a name is entered in the register of immortals; practice it for fifty years, and the gods of heaven bow in reverence, and one is ranked among the immortal host. If one does not earnestly practice in accordance with this, but does it sometimes and stops sometimes, practicing today and abandoning tomorrow; then, since one's dealings with people have gone awry, the field of the heart grows dark day by day; though one recites the scripture, the mind does not awaken. This is to profane Heaven, an offense not to be forgiven.”

In walking according to it, one must above all avoid “doing it sometimes and stopping sometimes, practicing today and abandoning tomorrow.” The work lies in unremitting perseverance, the same from first to last. This is where every practitioner must be on his guard.

The Illustrated Compendium on the Taishang Ganying Pian says: “When the human mind is still and unmoved, principle and desire have not yet taken form; there being no principle and no desire, there is of itself no fortune or misfortune. But once it stirs and shows itself in affairs, then fortune arises in accord with principle and misfortune gathers in accord with desire, like planting melons to get melons and planting beans to get beans — natural and not to be altered. Thus the coming of fortune and misfortune is summoned by the person himself; what door or path is there in it? This is why the ancients were diligent in examining themselves three times by day, and on guard in the four knowledges by night, cautious and fearful in the hour when no one sees and no one hears — it was nothing but the wish to hasten toward fortune and avoid calamity.”

[Three examinations] Constantly examining (reflecting upon) oneself from the three aspects of body, speech, and mind; it also means consciously examining oneself many times each day. [The four knowledges] Heaven knows, the gods know, I know, and you know. The Biography of Yang Zhen in the

Book of the Later Han records: Yang Zhen, styled Boqi, was a man of Huayin county in Hongnong commandery in the Eastern Han. He was just and incorruptible in his conduct, never scheming for private gain, a rare honest official. On his way to take up the post of governor of Donglai, Yang Zhen passed through Changyi. The magistrate of Changyi at that time, Wang Mi, was an official whom Yang Zhen had promoted when he himself served as inspector of Jingzhou. Hearing that Yang Zhen was passing through his district, and wishing to repay the kindness of that former promotion, Wang Mi went to pay his respects by day, and at night prepared ten jin of silver, intending to present it to Yang Zhen. Yang Zhen said to him: “We are old friends; I know your character well, yet you do not know mine. Why is that?” Wang Mi said: “It is the dead of night, and no one knows.” Yang Zhen said: “Heaven knows, the gods know, I know, and you know — how can you say no one knows?” Hearing this, Wang Mi withdrew in shame.

In cutting off evil and cultivating good, one must pay special attention to the fact that good and evil are of three kinds — of body, of speech, and of mind. Yet people, in cutting off evil, often value only the evil of the body while making light of the evil of speech and ignoring the evil of mind. In truth, the evil karma created by speech and by mind is most fearsome, for the evil of speech occurs far more often than the evil of the body, and the evil of mind occurs far more often still, so that “evil thoughts rise in shadowy swarms.” Moreover, the good and evil of body and speech spring from the good and evil of mind. This is explained in detail in the Annotations on the Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Meeting with the Kitchen God, and vividly illustrated with examples in The Way of Gathering Fortune and Dispelling Calamity. Therefore one must cut off not only the evil of the body but also the evil of speech and the evil of mind; one must increase not only the good of the body but also the good of speech and the good of mind. One must delight in goodness and delight in giving, and hate evil as one hates an enemy (hate one's own transgressions).
[Body, speech, and mind] Body refers to action — all the movements and deeds that issue from the body; speech refers to words; mind refers to thoughts.

Before a person gives rise to a thought, this mind is limpid and pure, neither good nor evil. Only when a thought stirs is there good, if it accords with principle, and evil, if it runs against principle. At first it is no more than a single thought, a single word, or a single act; but as days pile up and months accumulate, there comes the distinction between good person and evil person, and the retribution of gaining fortune or meeting calamity. Tracing it to its root, whether one gains fortune or meets calamity depends entirely on whether the thought first aroused was good or evil. Therefore one must be exceedingly careful about the arising of one's thoughts!

Chan Master Lingyuan of the Song dynasty said to Mr. Yichuan: calamity can give rise to fortune, and fortune can also give rise to calamity. Calamity can give rise to fortune because, when a person stands in peril and hardship, he urgently seeks safety, and probes deeply into the principle of safety, and above all is able to be wholeheartedly reverent and cautious; fortune can give rise to calamity because, when a person dwells in ease and pleasure, he indulges thoughts of greed and extravagance, and gives free rein to arrogance and slackness, and above all is often careless and contemptuous. (This is to say: by reverence and caution, calamity can give rise to fortune; by arrogance and slackness, fortune can give rise to calamity.)

In practicing the Taishang Ganying Pian, besides this textbook, the following books are very important, and may be read at the Online Buddhist Academy of the Rushi Xiuxing website and in its study gardens:
The Way of Gathering Fortune and Dispelling Calamity (A Vernacular Abridgment of the Compilation on the Ganying Pian)
Annotations on Liaofan's Four Lessons
Annotations on the Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Meeting with the Kitchen God
The Method of Preserving Wealth

blocks.text: Chapter 2: Taking Away Lifespan According to One's Faults

inline.s: [Therefore Heaven and Earth have spirits that oversee transgressions, and according to the gravity of what a person has done they take away his reckoning. When the reckoning is diminished, he becomes poor and ruined, meets with many sorrows and calamities, all people detest
(wù)
him, punishments and misfortunes follow him, auspicious celebrations shun him, and evil stars bring disaster upon him; when the reckoning is exhausted, he dies.]

Therefore Heaven and Earth have spirits that oversee transgressions, and according to the lightness or gravity of each person's offenses they take away his allotment of years. When the allotment is diminished, ill fortune comes upon him one after another: poverty and the ruin of his house, meeting with many sorrows and calamities, detested by all, with punishments and calamities following him, while auspicious and joyful affairs all shun him and the fierce evil stars send down disaster upon him; and once his allotment of years is wholly taken away, the hour of death arrives.
[Spirits that oversee transgressions] The deities who preside over human offenses and their punishments.
[Reckoning] Here “reckoning” is the reckoning of lifespan; the reckoning of lifespan is also called the number of years, or the years of life.
[Poor and ruined] Poor means without wealth, ruined means the household broken.
[Evil stars] The deities who preside over calamity and adversity.

A couplet at the Temple of the Eastern Peak says: “In the world of the living, the villain who hardens his heart and injures principle does it all himself; in the courts below, retribution — from ancient times to now, whom has it ever let pass?”

When Li Deng was eighteen he took the provincial examination and placed first. Yet by the age of fifty he had still not passed the metropolitan examination, and so he went to visit Dharma Master Ye Jing, asking him to look into the matter for him in the underworld. For this the Master called upon Emperor Zitong, and saw a clerk holding a register who said: “When Li Deng was first born, the Lord on High bestowed a jade seal upon him: at eighteen he would place first in the provincial examination (first in the whole province among the juren), at nineteen he would be zhuangyuan (first among the jinshi), and at fifty-three he would rise to the office of Right Chancellor. But after he passed the provincial examination, he spied upon the neighbor girl Zhang Yanniang and had her father Zhang Cheng thrown into prison. For this crime his fame and office were postponed ten years, and he was demoted to a jinshi of the second class. Afterward he seized his elder brother's house site and went to law over it; for this crime his fame and office were postponed another ten years, and he was demoted to the third class. At his lodging in Chang'an he violated the wife of a good man, Madam Zheng, and had her husband Zheng Baiyuan thrown into prison; for this crime his fame and office were postponed another ten years, and he was demoted to the fourth class. Afterward he again committed lewdness with the neighbor girl Wang Qingniang, doing evil without repentance, and his official register has already been erased!” Dharma Master Ye Jing told Li Deng all these words, and Li Deng died of shame and remorse.

Yan Guangzhong said: “Had this student Li not sought an inquiry in the underworld, then having passed the provincial examination while young, he would have run wild in arrogance and lewdness, thinking that his portion of fortune had reached its height! And onlookers might even have said: ‘With such arrogance and lewdness he still passed the examination!’ — and would instead have come to think the way of Heaven not worthy of belief.”

blocks.text: Chapter 3: The Gods Observe and Examine

inline.s: [Moreover, there are the divine lords of the Three Terraces and the Big Dipper, dwelling above a person's head, recording his evil deeds and taking away his period and reckoning. There are also the Three Corpse Spirits, within a person's body, who on every Keng-shen day ascend to the heavenly offices and report a person's offenses. On the last day of the lunar month, the Kitchen God does likewise.]

Moreover, there are the divine lords of the Three Terraces star and the divine lords of the Big Dipper star, who dwell above each person's head, recording every evil deed he commits and taking away his years of life (period and reckoning). There are also the Three Corpse Spirits within a person's body, who on every Keng-shen day (there is one Keng-shen day every sixty days) ascend to the heavenly offices (the government bureaus of Heaven) and memorialize a person's offenses. The Kitchen God of every household does likewise: on the last day of each lunar month he ascends to Heaven and memorializes the offenses of that household.

[The divine lords of the Three Terraces] The divine lords of the Three Terraces preside over a person's birth and death, longevity and early death. The Upper Terrace governs destiny (the Upper Terrace governs lifespan), the Middle Terrace governs fortune, and the Lower Terrace governs emolument. [Emolument] In ancient times the stipend of officials; that is, a person's economic income. [The divine lords of the Big Dipper] The divine lords of the Big Dipper command all spirits, direct the turning of the qi and the movements of fate, and weigh out death and life. When a person has offenses, they are entered in the register of evil, and their weight is measured, and his period and reckoning are taken away. [Period] In ancient reckoning of years, one period is twelve years. [Reckoning] Also one hundred days. [Period and reckoning] Here the term is used broadly to stand for the years of one's lifespan. [The Three Corpse Spirits] The upper corpse spirit, the Blue Maiden, named Peng Ju, dwells in a person's head, causing him many thoughts and desires, dimmed eyesight, and falling hair; the middle corpse spirit, the White Maiden, named Peng Zhi, dwells in a person's intestines, causing him to crave food, to be much forgetful, and to delight in doing evil; the lower corpse spirit, the Blood Maiden, named Peng Qiao, dwells in a person's feet, causing him to be addicted to lust and fond of killing, so that his limbs and organs are disturbed. They wish a person to die quickly, that they may go out and become ghosts and enjoy the offerings of blood and flesh; therefore on the Keng-shen day, while the person is asleep, they go with the seven po-souls within the body and ascend to the heavenly offices, and report that person's offenses.

[Keng-shen day] In ancient times the cycle of stems and branches was used to record years, months, and days. The stems and branches are the combined name of the heavenly stems and the earthly branches: the heavenly stems (jia, yi, bing, ding, wu, ji, geng, xin, ren, gui) and the earthly branches (zi, chou, yin, mao, chen, si, wu, wei, shen, you, xu, hai) combine to make sixty pairs, which form one cycle, called the sixty stems-and-branches or the sixty-flower cycle, also shortened to the flower cycle. When days are recorded by the stems and branches, there is one Keng-shen day in every flower cycle (every sixty days). [Ze
zhé
Always; invariably.
This passage means that throughout a person's life, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there are always gods and spirits observing and examining him.

[Whatever offense a person has, if great it takes away a period, if small it takes away a reckoning. These offenses, great and small, number several hundred; whoever wishes to seek long life must first guard against them.]

Whatever offense a person may have, if it is great, then a period is taken away (one period is twelve years of lifespan); if it is small, then a reckoning is taken away (one reckoning is one hundred days of lifespan). These offenses, great and small, are the several hundred matters listed below; whoever wishes to seek long life must first guard against them.
[Several hundred matters] Referring to the many and various offenses listed in chapters five and six, from “acts contrary to righteousness” down to “death too comes upon him.”

blocks.text: Chapter 4: Advancing in the Way and Cultivating Good

inline.s: [What accords with the Way, advance toward; what does not accord with the Way, retreat from. Do not tread the path of evil; do not deceive in the dark chamber. Accumulate virtue and build up merit; have a compassionate heart toward all things. Be loyal, filial, friendly, and brotherly; rectify yourself and transform others. Pity the orphan and comfort the widow; revere the aged and cherish the young. Even insects and grass are not to be harmed.]

What accords with the Way — press boldly forward; what does not accord with the Way — resolutely retreat. Do not walk the crooked byways (do not tread the path of evil); even where no one can see, do nothing that cannot bear the light (do not deceive in the dark chamber). Accumulate virtue and build up merit; have a compassionate heart toward all things. Be loyal, filial, friendly, and brotherly; rectify yourself and transform others. Pity the orphan and comfort the widow; revere the aged and cherish the young. Even insects and grass must not be harmed.

[Accumulate virtue and build up merit] Ceaselessly raise up one's own nature (accumulating virtue), and ceaselessly rescue those in hardship (building up merit). [Have a compassionate heart toward all things] The word “things” here means people other than oneself, or the circumstances that stand over against one. [Friendly and brotherly] This speaks of the relation between brothers: the elder brother loves the younger (friendly), and the younger brother respects and loves the elder (brotherly, ti).

Chan Master Yangqi served as the monastery administrator under Chan Master Shishuang. Reading the scriptures at night, he bought lamp oil of his own for himself, and never privately used the oil of the community (that is, the monastery's). Chan Master Zhihao (Baoshou was his other name) served as administrator under Chan Master Wuzu Shijie. Wuzu had a cold ailment, and needed ginger and brown sugar boiled into a paste to take regularly. The attendant came to the storeroom to seek these two things, and Chan Master Zhihao said: “How can the community's public goods be used privately? Bring money and buy them!” Wuzu at once sent someone with money to buy them, and thought very highly of Chan Master Zhihao. Later, when Dongshan lacked an abbot, someone asked Wuzu to recommend one. Wuzu said: “The fellow who sold his ginger will do.”

A eulogy says: “Yangqi's lamp gave light through a thousand ages; Baoshou's ginger stings sharp for ten thousand years.” (This praises the spirit of “Yangqi's lamp and Baoshou's ginger”: Yangqi used lamp oil keeping public and private strictly apart; Baoshou would not use the community's ginger to buy the abbot's good will.)

Master Yinguang, in the first of his Replies to Layman Shao Huiyuan, told of his own experience: “When I reached Lotus Flower Temple in Hubei, I asked for the hardest post in the monastery (stoking coal, boiling drinking water for more than forty people, day and night without rest. The water I had to carry myself, and the coal cinders I had to carry out myself. Because I had not yet received the precepts, that I was permitted to stay there was already great compassion on their part). In the fourth month of the next year the associate temple officer went home, and the storekeeper fell ill; the abbot saw that I was honest and had me look after the storeroom. The accounts of silver and money the abbot himself attended to. When I had first left home, I had seen the couplet ‘Yangqi's lamp gave light through a thousand ages, Baoshou's ginger stings sharp for ten thousand years,’ and the rule in the Vinaya for Novices on the retribution for stealing the community's goods, and my heart was greatly in awe. Whenever I handled sugary foods, if my hands became sticky or smelled of them, I never dared use my tongue to lick them, but only wiped them with paper.”

Ouyang Xiu, in his Tablet at the Shuanggang Grave, recorded his mother's instruction: When I first married into your family, your father had been in mourning for his mother only one year. At the year-end sacrifice to the ancestors he would always say with tears: “However rich the offerings, they are not equal to the poorest care given while one was alive.” If by chance he had good wine and food, he would again say with tears: “In former days, when my mother was here, we often had not enough; now that we are well-off and have more than enough, there is no way to let her taste it!” At first, when I met with such feelings, I thought it was only because his mourning had not long ended. But afterward it was always so, right up to his death. Though I never had the chance to serve my mother-in-law, from this one thing I could see how deeply your father honored his parents.

Shi Zuo and Shi You were two brothers, both of them prefects. After they resigned office and lived at home, a dispute over land grew into angry words, and though friends and kin day after day tried to settle matters for them, they could not dissolve it. Yan Feng of the same county was known for his filial devotion and his kindness and love; he served his elder brother as he would a father, and in relieving and caring for others there was nothing he did not do. By chance he met Shi You on a boat, and Shi You began to tell him of the dispute over the land. Master Yan knit his brows and said: “My own brother is weak-willed, and I am just now troubled over this very matter. If he were like your elder brother, he could take every field I have from me — what sorrow would I have left?” And with that he wept. Shi You was moved and awakened, and taking Yan Feng with him he went straight to his elder brother's dwelling, and weeping and bowing he deeply repented and blamed himself. Shi Zuo too wept and consoled him, and each yielded land to the other; and so they were loving brothers to the end of their lives.

Comment: Mr. Yuan Junzai, in his Yuan Family Precepts for the World, says: “Bones and flesh falling out of harmony begins in some very small matter, and ends in a degree from which there is no dissolving it. This is because after the falling out each side nurses his anger and will not bow his head. If one person can first lower himself and be the first to apologize, then the dealings between them will of themselves be as they were before.” Reading this, one believes it all the more.

[One should commiserate with others' misfortune and rejoice in others' good. Relieve others' urgency and rescue others' peril. See others' gain as one's own gain. See others' loss as one's own loss. Do not publicize others' shortcomings; do not vaunt one's own strengths. Suppress evil and promote good; put aside the many and take the little. Bear insult without resentment; receive favor as if startled. Confer kindness without seeking return; give to others without regret.]

One should pity the misfortune of others and delight in their prosperity. Relieve others in their urgent need, and rescue others from danger. See another's gain as one's own gain. See another's loss as one's own loss. Do not make known another's shortcomings, and do not display one's own strengths. Stop evil and spread good; yield the larger portion and take the smaller. Bear insult without resentment; be startled by favor. Confer kindness without seeking repayment; give to others without afterward regretting it.
[Be startled by favor] When one receives favor, courtesy, or preferential treatment, to feel deeply uneasy that one has not done enough to deserve it.

Xu Shuwei of the Song dynasty prayed every day to pass the metropolitan examination. He dreamed that a god said to him: “To pass the jinshi examination you must rely on hidden virtue.” Xu Shuwei reflected that his family was poor and he had no means, and that the practice of medicine was all he had. So he applied himself bitterly to the medical books, and in time he mastered the art of healing. No matter whether the sick were of high station or low, he hurried to diagnose and treat them, and the number he saved alive was very great. Thus his fame grew ever greater, and his good heart grew ever more urgent, and afterward he passed the jinshi examination.

Xue Bao served his parents with the utmost filial devotion. After his parents passed away, his younger brothers asked to divide the property and live apart, and Xue Bao could not stop them. When the household was divided, of the servants and maids he asked only for the old ones, saying: “We have been together so long that they are used to the way things are done.” Of the vessels and utensils he took the old and worn ones, saying: “These are what I have always used, and I am used to them.” Of the fields he asked only for the barren ones, saying: “These I farmed as a boy, and my heart clings to them.” He let his younger brothers take whatever they wished. Later his younger brothers one after another went bankrupt, and he again gave them relief.

[The one called a good person — all people revere him, the way of Heaven protects him, fortune and emolument follow him, all evil things keep far from him, the gods and spirits guard him, whatever he undertakes is surely accomplished, and immortal-hood may be hoped for. Whoever seeks to become a heaven-immortal should establish one thousand three hundred good deeds. Whoever seeks to become an earth-immortal should establish three hundred good deeds.]

One who fulfills all the articles above — this is what is meant by a good person. All people revere him, the way of Heaven protects him, fortune and emolument follow him, all evil things keep far from him, the gods and spirits guard him, whatever he undertakes is surely accomplished, and there is still the hope of becoming an immortal. Whoever seeks to become a heaven-immortal must complete one thousand three hundred good deeds. Whoever seeks to become an earth-immortal must complete three hundred good deeds.
[The one called] That which is spoken of; what is meant by.

blocks.text: Chapter 5: The Various Offenses
1. Acting Contrary to Righteousness

inline.s: [If one acts contrary to righteousness and walks against principle.]
If one acts contrary to righteousness and walks against principle.

Above, the text spoke of good minds and good deeds and their good retribution; now, with the words “if one” it turns the tone and speaks of the many kinds of evil minds and evil deeds and their evil retribution.

If one acts contrary to righteousness and walks against principle” — this single passage is the general statement of this chapter and of the next, “Heaped Up Evil Retribution.” What follows, down to “death too comes upon him,” enumerates the many particular minds and acts of “acting contrary to righteousness and walking against principle,” that is, the many offenses that summon calamity and take away lifespan, the several hundred matters great and small of which it was said above that “whoever wishes to seek long life must first guard against them.”

[Regard evil as ability, and endure in cruelty and harm. Secretly injure the good; covertly insult ruler and parents. Slight one's teacher; betray the work one serves. Deceive the ignorant; slander one's fellow students. Be false, accusing, deceitful, and hypocritical; attack and expose one's kin. Be hard and unkind, fierce and perverse, self-willed.]

To regard doing evil as ability, and to endure in cruelty and harm. To scheme and secretly injure the good, and covertly deceive ruler and parents. To slight one's teacher, and to be careless in the duties one serves. To deceive the ignorant, and to slander one's fellow students. To be false, accusing, deceitful, and hypocritical; to attack and expose one's own kin. To be hard and violent, fierce and perverse, and self-willed.

[False, accusing, deceitful, and hypocritical] To be without any foundation is “false”; to fabricate and defame is “accusing”; to deceive by cunning schemes is “deceitful”; to feign what one is not in order to cheat the world is “hypocritical.” Taken together, these four amount to insincerity. One should know: sincerity is the way of Heaven; to seek sincerity is the way of man. Now to cast aside sincerity and be false, accusing, deceitful, and hypocritical — is this not to run against the way of Heaven and lose the way of man? To harbor such thoughts and act in such ways makes the mind very toilsome and the affairs very perilous, and is the mark of the thinnest fortune under Heaven, and one will surely fall into the three evil paths (animal, hungry ghost, and hell). Therefore a sincere and honest heart is the basic standard of being human. [To feign what one is not] To deliberately go against ordinary feeling, in order to appear lofty or to set oneself apart from others. [To attack and expose (jié)] To uncover another's faults or private secrets and attack him for them. [Kin] Relatives of the same descent. [Fierce and perverse, self-willed] Fierce and perverse, and considering oneself always right. [Perverse] (Of temperament, speech, or conduct) contrary and unreasonable.

blocks.text: 2. Doing Evil and Wickedness

inline.s: [Right and wrong not properly judged; likes and dislikes perversely placed. Oppress subordinates to win merit; flatter superiors to court their favor. Receive kindness without gratitude; nurse resentment without end. Despise the people of Heaven; disturb the governance of the state. Reward the unrighteous; punish the innocent. Kill to take wealth; topple others to take their place. Slay the surrendered and execute the submissive; disparage the upright and push aside the worthy. Bully the orphan and coerce the widow; set aside the law and take bribes.]

Right and wrong are not distinguished and are handled improperly; one inclines to evil and turns from the right, walking the contrary road. One squeezes those below to win merit for oneself, and caters to the will of those above to win their favor. One receives kindness without gratitude, and nurses resentment without cease. One despises the common people and throws the governance of the state into disorder. One rewards those who are unrighteous, and punishes those who are innocent. One kills a man to take his wealth, and ruins a man to seize his place. One puts to death those who have surrendered, disparages upright gentlemen, and pushes aside worthy and capable ministers. One bullies orphans and coerces widows, and sets the law aside to take bribes.

[Likes and dislikes perversely placed] To incline to evil and turn from the right, walking the contrary road. “Incline” means to move toward; “turn” means to move the other way; “perverse” means to run counter; “placed” means what is proper. [The people of Heaven] The common people. [Courting their favor] Also written “courting their will”: to cater to the will of those above. [Disturb the governance of the state] To propose and carry out policies and laws that ruin the state and bring calamity on the people. [Innocent] Those who have committed no crime.

In the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, heavy autumn rains damaged the crops, and only Liu Zao, the county magistrate of Weinan, reported that the young grain in his county had suffered no loss. The emperor was suspicious and ordered the censor Zhu Yi to go and inspect, and in fact more than three thousand qing had been damaged. The emperor sighed: “A county magistrate is the official who presides over the livelihood of the common people. If there were no loss, he ought even so to report a loss, so that the people might pay less tax; yet now his indifference to the people's livelihood has gone as far as this!” He at once demoted Liu Zao to be commandant of Nanpu, and on the way to his post Liu Zao died.

Jun Buyi served as governor of the capital region (the chief administrator of the metropolitan district, with authority equivalent to that of a commandery governor). When he came home after reviewing cases, his mother would ask whether he had redressed any wrongs and how many men he had saved alive. If there had been many redresses, his mother was greatly pleased; if there had been none, she would often be angry and refuse to eat. That is why Jun Buyi, in office, was strict but never cruel.

Han Yi served as prefect of Bozhou, and his second son served as judge of the Western Capital; the son came home to visit his parents. Han Yi was delighted and called together his colleagues and subordinates for a banquet, with kinsmen and sons of the family all seated there. Suddenly he asked about a difficult case in the Western Capital that had been submitted to the court for deliberation and decision — what had the particulars been? His second son thought for a long while and could not recall it, whereupon Han Yi called for a cane and cursed him, saying: “You have charge of twenty-one prefectures; every matter, great or small, must be examined to the bottom and with care. A matter as grave as sentencing a man to death you cannot even remember — how much less the idle and petty affairs!” He was determined to beat this unworthy, disobedient son, and only the guests' strenuous efforts at dissuasion stopped him.
