Comment: To educate good ministers for the court and good officials for the people — only this can be called “kindly teaching” with respect to the family. Weighed in the balance, no merit is greater than this! Is not bringing fortune to one's descendants through doing good and accumulating virtue the deepest “kindness”? Is not setting up one's person and one's conduct as a model for others the most fundamental “teaching”? Those who love their children should pay especial heed to this!

[Take the straight for the crooked and the crooked for the straight. Make what is light into something heavy; seeing a man put to death, add anger. Know a fault and not change it; know what is good and not do it. Bring guilt upon oneself and drag others in; block up the arts and techniques. Mock and slander the sages and worthies; encroach upon and mistreat the moral.]

Crooked and straight are turned upside down, and cases are decided by favoritism. A light offense is given a heavy punishment; when a condemned man is put to death, one does not pity him but is angry with him. One knows one's faults and does not change them; one knows what is good and does not do it. Having committed a crime oneself, one turns and bites at others to get free. One obstructs the arts and skills of others and cuts off their living. One mocks and ridicules the sages and worthies of past and present, and encroaches upon and mistreats those who have moral virtue.

[Seeing a man put to death, add anger] When a man is being executed, not to pity him but to be angry with him — this is truly cruel beyond measure! Ouyang Xiu, in his Tablet at the Shuanggang Grave, recorded his mother's instruction: When your father was in office, he once sat by candlelight at night reading the case files, and several times he stopped and sighed. I asked him why, and he said: “This is a case carrying the death sentence; I wished to find a way of life for him and could not.” I asked: “Can a way of life be found for a condemned man?” He said: “If one seeks a way of life for him and can find none, then neither the dead man nor I will have any regret. And besides, seeking a way of life, one sometimes finds it! It is precisely because some are pardoned that one understands how those who were put to death without earnest inquiry must bear a lingering grievance. Constantly seeking a way of life for the condemned, one still cannot avoid killing some by mistake — how much worse that in this world there are always those who wish to put a prisoner to death!” [Block up the arts and techniques] “Arts and techniques” refers to such skills as medicine, divination, astrology, physiognomy, and alchemy in ancient times. Here “blocking up the arts and techniques” means abusing one's authority to obstruct the common people from supporting their families by their skills. Arts and techniques that harm society and the people are not included in this.

Jing Jiangjin of Hangzhou served in the Chaozhou office of the Lingnan region. He and his father were both deeply convinced of the principle of divine response; a copy of the Treatise of Response and Retribution always lay upon the table, and they recited it morning and evening. By this time Jing Jiangjin was past forty, had grown indifferent to fame and an official career, and, captivated by the scenery of Chaozhou and well paid besides, no longer planned to sit for the imperial examinations. In the xinmao year of the Qianlong reign there was a metropolitan examination in the capital for the jinshi degree. His father wrote one letter after another urging him home to prepare to go to the capital, but Jing Jiangjin declined again and again and was set on giving up the examination. His father's last letter said: “If you do not come back at once, you are gravely unfilial.” With no alternative, Jing Jiangjin returned home in low spirits and then went to the capital to sit the examination. As it turned out, he passed as the second name on the jinshi list (the bangyan). Not long afterward an imperial decree appointed him prefect of Chaozhou — truly a wish fulfilled! The reason was that before the metropolitan examination Jing Jiangjin had handled a case of a falsely accused theft and thereby saved the lives of fifty-seven people. Had he not practiced the Treatise of Response and Retribution day by day, how could he have thrown himself wholeheartedly into overturning a wrongful case?

The Grand Historian Xu says: This is one who does not dare to punish the innocent, one who does not dare to make the straight crooked or the crooked straight, or to make a light matter heavy — a truly benevolent man! Since he was able to fulfill his cherished desire to love the people, Heaven too caused such a benevolent man to realize his wish.

blocks.text: 3. Killing Creatures and Harming People

inline.s: Shooting birds on the wing, chasing beasts that run away; / Digging out hibernating insects, startling the birds that roost; / Filling in burrows and overturning nests, / Wounding the unborn and breaking the eggs.

Shooting and killing flying birds, chasing and seizing running beasts. Digging out hibernating insects, startling roosting birds in the night. Filling in the insects' burrows, overturning birds' nests, wounding the pregnant and breaking their eggs.
[Hibernating (
zhe
) insects]
Insects that hide in the soil to pass the winter.
[Wounding the unborn] Harming animals that are pregnant.
A verse says: “O, do not shoot the bird upon the bough; / Her young ones in the nest await her now.”

Wishing that others may fail, destroying their success; / Endangering others to make oneself secure, diminishing others to profit oneself; / Exchanging the good for the evil, setting aside the public good for private gain.

Wishing only that others may err, ruining and defeating others' success. Endangering others to make oneself secure, diminishing others to benefit oneself. Passing off the inferior as the superior, and for private ends setting aside the public good.

[Endangering others to make oneself secure] Framing others in order to consolidate one's own position. [Diminishing others to benefit oneself] Damaging the reputation of others in order to make oneself shine, or deducting from others' possessions to increase one's own profit. [Exchanging the good for the evil] Taking a bad thing and secretly substituting it for a good one, or passing off inferior goods as superior goods.

Stealing others' abilities, concealing others' goodness; / Exposing others' ugliness, prying into others' private affairs; / Wasting others' goods and wealth, estranging others' flesh and blood; / Seizing what others love, helping others to do wrong; / Indulging one's will to wield power, humiliating others to gain victory; / Ruining others' crops, destroying others' marriages.

Stealing the accomplishments of others, obscuring the talent of others. Displaying the faults of others, attacking the private affairs of others. Consuming the goods and wealth of others, estranging the flesh and blood of others. Seizing what others hold dear, helping others to do wrong. Indulging one's will and wielding power, humiliating others in order to win. Injuring the crops of others, destroying the marriages of others.

[Stealing others' abilities] Stealing the accomplishments of others, such as claiming credit that is not one's own, plagiarizing the writing of others or the results of their research, and so on. [Indulging one's will to wield power] Letting loose one's own inclinations and lording it over others with power.

blocks.text: 4. Arrogance and Cruelty

inline.s: Rich through wrongful means yet arrogant, escaped through wrongful means yet shameless; / Claiming others' favors, shifting one's own faults; / Laying disaster on others, selling one's evil; / Buying false reputation, harboring a treacherous heart; / Baffling the strengths of others, shielding one's own weaknesses; / Relying on power to coerce and threaten, letting loose violence to injure and kill.

Gaining wealth by wrongful means (by improper methods — such as lending at interest to take profit, founding a household through harshness, adulterating goods with falsehood, deceiving and cheating, or building an enterprise by sly and sinister ways — and so becoming rich), yet remaining arrogant and overbearing; escaping punishment by wrongful means (by improper methods — such as bribing officials or framing others — and so escaping punishment), yet being utterly without shame. Claiming the favors of others as one's own, shifting the blame onto others; laying disaster on others, selling one's evil to entrap people. Deceiving the world and stealing a reputation (buying false reputation), harboring a treacherous heart. Baffling the strengths of others, covering over one's own weaknesses. Relying on power to coerce and threaten, letting loose violence to injure and kill.

The character “couple” (gou) in “rich through wrongful means yet arrogant, escaped through wrongful means yet shameless” is the same as the “couple” in “make no wrongful gain when facing wealth, make no wrongful escape when facing peril” — it means contrary to what is right and reasonable. The meaning of “rich through wrongful means yet arrogant, escaped through wrongful means yet shameless” is: to grow rich through means contrary to what is right and yet remain arrogant and overbearing; to escape punishment through means contrary to what is right and yet be utterly without shame.

The meaning of “when facing wealth, make no wrongful gain; when facing peril, make no wrongful escape” is: when you encounter wealth, do not acquire it contrary to what is right; when you encounter peril, do not flee contrary to what is right. In other words: in the face of money, remain incorruptibly self-possessed; in the face of danger, put justice and courage first. These two sentences come from the Record of Rites, in the section “Curly Etiquette” (Quli): “When facing wealth, make no wrongful gain; when facing peril, make no wrongful escape; in argument do not insist on winning; in dividing goods do not insist on much.” (Translation: in the face of money remain incorruptibly self-possessed; in the face of danger put justice and courage first; when arguing with others do not insist on victory; when dividing property do not insist on getting more.)

[Selling one's evil] Passing evil to others like a commodity, for example helping others to devise evil schemes, to lay traps, and so on. [Baffling the strengths of others, shielding one's own weaknesses] Hindering and obstructing others from exercising their abilities, covering over and disguising the shortcomings of one's own abilities. [Do not insist on winning in argument] When arguing with others, do not insist on winning. “Arguing” here means, in ancient usage, disputation. When one argues with others, it is in order to arrive at truth, because truth becomes clearer the more it is argued. Yet if one is not careful, an argument easily degenerates into a contest of temper; at that point the debate no longer pursues truth but each side merely defends its own position, and so it becomes a matter of winning rather than of truth — and if one then goes so far as to speak rudely and hurl abuse, it becomes utterly meaningless.

The Record of Rites says: “When facing wealth, make no wrongful gain.” In Huangshi, Hubei Province, an old lady surnamed Guo, over seventy years old, found seven thousand yuan in cash while scavenging, and without hesitation handed it over to the police. After hobbling for more than an hour she found the duty officer, then counted the money together with the officer, then guided the officer to the scene to conduct an investigation, then returned to the station to give a statement — keeping at it for several hours. Only after completing all the prescribed formalities did Old Lady Guo bashfully say to the duty officer: “Officer, I have not yet had breakfast; could you lend me one yuan so that I may buy two steamed buns to eat?”

When the celebrated scientist Qian Xuesen was studying at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the preeminent master of aeronautics and astronautics, Theodore von Karman, was his advisor. One day, when Qian Xuesen told his advisor of a result he had spent much time and effort to bring to success, the advisor listened a long while without understanding, then interrupted impatiently: “This is impossible; you must have made a mistake.” Qian Xuesen was exceedingly dejected over this. Just as he was racking his brains over how to get his teacher to change his mind, von Karman knocked at the door, bowed deeply to Qian Xuesen, and said with a face full of apology: “I thought about it all night; I feel your research result is correct. I apologize to you.” Some considered von Karman's act of apology uncalled for, holding that a teacher need not apologize to his student; but von Karman replied: “I am bowing to truth and to science — this is the minimum morality of a scientist.”

Cutting and tailoring without cause, slaughtering and cooking without ritual; / Scattering and wasting the five grains, troubling and oppressing the people; / Destroying others' homes, seizing their wealth and treasure; / Breaching the dikes and setting fires, harming the people's dwellings; / Throwing plans into confusion, defeating others' undertakings; / Damaging others' tools and vessels, leaving them without what they need.

Making new garments for no reason at all (not knowing how to cherish one's blessings), slaughtering and cooking livestock without necessity (not cherishing the lives of creatures). Wasting grain (scattering and discarding the five grains), troubling and disturbing the common people. Destroying the homes of others, seizing their wealth and treasure. Breaching the dikes and setting fire, harming people's dwellings. Casting plans into confusion (throwing arrangements into disorder), defeating others' undertakings (causing others not to succeed). Damaging the tools and vessels of others, leaving them short of what they need.

[Slaughtering and cooking without ritual] Slaughtering and cooking livestock at a time other than for sacrifice. “Ritual” here means sacrificial offering; “slaughter and cook” means killing and cooking livestock. In ancient times animals were killed for sacrifice, and only after the offering was completed and the offering removed could the people eat of it. A person prizes his own life greatly, and so should also cherish the lives of animals. The way of Heaven revolves: today you kill him, another day he kills you; today you eat him, another day he eats you. Wrong for wrong, revenge for revenge — when will it ever end? A poem says: “Scarcely has it passed the three-inch tongue — / Who still can taste the sour or the salt? / Greed and craving create the karma of killing; / The retribution is enough to chill the heart.” Another says: “The broth in the bowl for a thousand hundred years; / The wrong is deep as the sea, the hatred hard to level. / Would you know of the swords and blades of this world? / Just listen to the butcher's door in the middle of the night.” [Breaching the dikes] Destroying the embankments. [Damaging others' tools and vessels, leaving them without what they need] Deliberately damaging others' tools and vessels so that when the time comes they have nothing usable.

blocks.text: 5. Jealousy and Curses of Ruin

inline.s: Seeing others honored and noble, wishing them exiled and degraded; / Seeing others wealthy, wishing their families broken and their goods scattered; / Seeing a fair woman, conceiving a heart to covet her; / Owing another goods and wealth, wishing him dead.

Seeing others in glory and splendor, wishing them banished and degraded. Seeing others rich, wishing their families ruined and their members scattered. Seeing a fair woman, giving rise to a lustful heart and desiring a secret affair with her. Owing another money and goods, wishing him dead.

When asking and seeking go unfulfilled, straightway giving rise to cursing and hatred; / Seeing others at a disadvantage, straightway speaking of their faults; / Seeing others with imperfect bodies and laughing at them, / Seeing others with praiseworthy abilities and repressing them.

When seeking and requesting go unfulfilled, straightway cursing and resenting. Seeing others suffer loss, taking the chance to proclaim their faults (throwing a stone upon one who has fallen into a well). Seeing others with incomplete bodies and mocking them, seeing others with outstanding abilities and demeaning them.
[Asking and seeking]
To request; to seek.

blocks.text: 6. Venomous Wickedness and Crafty Treachery

inline.s: Burying poppets to bewitch people, using poison to kill trees; / Nursing anger against one's teacher, opposing one's father and elder brothers; / Taking by force and demanding by force, fond of encroaching and fond of seizing; / Plundering to grow rich, using craft and deceit to seek promotion; / Rewards and punishments unjust, indulgence and pleasure beyond measure; / Cruel and tyrannical toward one's subordinates, threatening and frightening others.
Using sorcery to bewitch people, using poison to kill trees. Nursing resentment against one's teacher, defying one's father and elder brothers. Taking by force and demanding by force, being fond (
hao

, that is, fond) of encroaching and of seizing. Plundering (taking captives and robbing goods) to grow rich, using craft and deceit to seek promotion. Rewards and punishments unjust, ease and pleasure carried too far (beyond due measure). Cruel and tyrannical toward one's subordinates, threatening and intimidating others.

[Burying poppets to bewitch people] Burying in the ground a puppet on which one has written a name and the eight characters of the birth date and hour, in order to bewitch the person; this is also called “sorcery of poisoning spirits.” This is an evil art, and by law the offender should be put to death by beheading. “Gu” (a poisonous insect that harms people) is here used as a metaphor for the puppet that bewitches people; “oppress people” means to “bewitch people,” bringing calamity upon them by sorcery. For example, in Dream of the Red Chamber, Concubine Zhao bribes the witch Ma Daopo to cut out paper figures and bewitch Xifeng and Jia Baoyu. [The eight characters of the birth date and hour] The year, month, day, and hour of a person's birth. “Birth date”: the day of birth; “eight characters”: the heavenly stems and earthly branches governing the year, month, day, and hour of birth, each of these four items having two characters, for a total of eight characters.

blocks.text: 7. Violence and Slander

inline.s: Resenting Heaven and blaming others, rebuking the wind and cursing the rain; / Stirring up quarrels and contentions, frivolously pursuing factions; / Heeding the words of wives and concubines, defying the instructions of parents; / Gaining the new and forgetting the old, saying one thing while meaning another; / Greedy to seize wealth, deceiving and hoodwinking one's superiors.

Resenting Heaven and blaming others, rebuking the wind and cursing the rain. Eggng on mutual quarrels, instigating lawsuits (going to court); forming factions and bands, using force to oppress the weak. Heeding the slander of wives and concubines, defying the instruction of parents. Gaining the new and forgetting the old, saying yes while meaning no (a hypocrite). Embezzling and falsely claiming money and goods, deceiving and hoodwinking one's superiors and elders.

[Resenting Heaven and blaming others] When one meets with setbacks or problems, blaming Heaven and reproaching others. “To blame” means to resent, to lay the fault upon. [Rebuking the wind and cursing the rain] When the wind and rain do not suit one's wishes, scolding and complaining about them. [Stirring up quarrels and contentions] Eggng on mutual fights, instigating lawsuits (going to court), and so fishing for gain from them. [Gaining the new and forgetting the old] From small things such as clothes and utensils to great things such as friendship and kinship; within the household from wives and concubines down to servants and maids — all have the new and the old. If one delights in the new and tires of the old, gaining the new and forgetting the old, then that person is exceedingly fickle and ungrateful. Therefore the sages of old have said: “Rather than forge new friendships, honor (be attentive to) old good ones.” Once the king of Chu issued an edict seeking a lost shoe, saying: “I went out together with the shoes I wore, yet they did not return with me — how it grieves me!” From that time on, no one in the state of Chu dared to cast away old things. So the king of Chu was indeed a man of feeling through the ages, and a man who understood the Way through the ages!

Fabricating evil speech, slandering innocent people; / Defaming others while claiming to be upright, cursing the gods while claiming to be righteous; / Abandoning compliance and imitating rebellion, turning from kin toward strangers; / Pointing to Heaven and Earth to attest a base heart, / Calling on the gods and spirits to witness obscene deeds.

Fabricating evil speech (words that injure people), slandering good people. Defaming others while calling oneself straightforward, reviling the gods while calling oneself just. Abandoning compliance and imitating rebellion, turning from kin toward strangers. Pointing to Heaven and Earth as witness to a base heart, foolishly trying to show oneself without fault; calling on the gods and spirits to examine an obscene and ugly affair, foolishly trying to prove one's innocence. (This is to say: harboring a sinister heart and having done shameful things, one nevertheless borrows Heaven, Earth, gods, and spirits to prove one's sincerity and innocence.)
[Innocent people]
People without guilt, good citizens.

[Abandoning compliance and imitating rebellion] Following the principle of Heaven is called compliance; defying the principle of Heaven is called rebellion. The compliant obtain good fortune; the rebellious meet with calamity. “Abandoning compliance and imitating rebellion” means casting aside the principle of Heaven (setting it aside without regard) and giving oneself over to words and deeds that defy it. [Turning from kin toward strangers] Confucius said: “One who does not love his own kin yet loves others is called one who perverts virtue; one who does not respect his own kin yet respects others is called one who perverts ritual.” Now to turn from kin toward strangers stems either from following private favoritism in gratitude and enmity, or from taking a view of human feeling and worldly advantage. To pervert virtue and to pervert ritual are exceedingly grave — these are fundamental heavy offenses, and their retribution is very bitter.

blocks.text: 8. Stinginess, Avarice, and Greed

inline.s: Giving and then regretting it, borrowing and never returning; / Seeking beyond one's lot, using force to lay down one's schemes; / Lust and desire carried to excess, a venomous heart with a kind face; / Feeding people with filthy food, deluding the masses with heterodox ways.

Giving away goods and then regretting it, borrowing goods and not returning them. Scheming and seeking beyond one's own lot, abusing one's authority to show power and lay down measures. Lust carried to excess, a venomous heart with a kind face (honey on the lips, a sword in the heart). Feeding the poor with filthy food (dirty, spoiled food), deluding the masses with evil ways (heterodox paths).

[Borrowing and not returning] Here “lend” (jia) also has the meaning of “borrow.” [Using force to lay down one's schemes] Abusing one's authority to show power and lay down measures, doing one's utmost to squeeze one's subordinates and the common people.

In the Liu-Song period, Xi Xiandu held the office of Cavalier Attendant of the Interior. Emperor Xiaowu once ordered him to oversee and direct the laborers, and he was harsh, tyrannical, and unreasonable; toward the workers he would, at the slightest pretext, beat and flog them, and no matter whether the weather was bitter cold or scorching hot, or whether it rained or snowed, he would not allow the workers to halt and rest. Many workers, unable to bear the suffering, killed themselves; and Xi Xiandu, when his misdeeds came to light, was likewise put to death by imperial decree.

Short the ruler, scant the measure, light the scale, small the pint; / Mixing the false into the true, seizing unlawful profit; / Pressing the good into servitude, cheating and tricking the foolish; / Greedy and insatiable, swearing oaths to claim one is right.

Short the ruler, scant the measure, light the scale, small the pint. Mixing the false into the true (for instance, adding water to wine) to reap exorbitant profit. Pressing the good into servitude, employing crafty schemes to deceive people. Greedy and never satiated, swearing oaths and making vows to falsely claim that one is in the right.
[Short the ruler, scant the measure, light the scale, small the pint] When selling goods,

using a short ruler (for example, a cloth-seller's yard stick shorter than the standard), a scant measure (for example, a wine ladle smaller than the standard), a light scale (a seller's balance lighter than the standard), and a small sheng (a rice-seller's sheng or dou smaller than the standard), in order to profit unlawfully.

[Pressing the good into servitude] Using power to make women of good families one's own maidservants, and even selling good women into prostitution. [Cheating and tricking] “Cheat” means deceiving people so that they neither know nor see; “trick” has the look of being quick and clever. To lay traps by crafty schemes so that people fall into them is called “cheating and tricking.” [Swearing oaths to claim one is right] Swearing and vowing to God that one is right and righteous. “Swearing” means taking an oath before the gods; “to claim one is right” means to declare that one's reason is correct.

blocks.text: 9. Anger and Quarrels, Disobedience

inline.s: Loving wine and rebelling in disorder, flesh and blood quarrelling in anger; / Men not loyal and good, women not gentle and compliant; / Not in harmony within the household, not respectful to one's husband; / Ever fond of boasting, constantly practicing jealousy; / Wanting in conduct toward wife and children, failing in courtesy toward the in-laws.

Drinking to excess and being dazed and disorderly (acting wildly), quarrelling in anger with one's kin. Men not loyal and good, women not gentle and compliant. Husbands treating wives without kindness, wives not respecting their husbands. Husband and wife fond of contending with each other and boasting, constantly jealous and suspicious. The master of the house behaving improperly toward wife and children, the daughter-in-law not filial to her father- and mother-in-law.
[Father- and mother-in-law] The name for the parents of one's husband (the father- and mother-in-law).

Disrespecting the departed spirits, defying the commands of one's superiors; / Doing what is useless, harboring a heart turned outward; / Cursing oneself and cursing others, hating some and loving others partially.

Disrespecting one's departed parents and ancestors (the former spirits), defying the instructions and commands of one's elders. Doing what is of no benefit to the state, the family, and society; toward the state and family, toward kin and friends, harboring an outward-turned heart (eating from within and leaking to without). Nursing resentment, cursing oneself and others; pulling together one faction and striking down another (partial hatred and partial love).
[An outward-turned heart]

A minister deceiving the ruler, a son defying his parents, husband and wife turning their backs on each other, brothers robbing one another, friends overthrowing one another — all are driven by an outward-turned heart.
[Cursing oneself and cursing others] Nursing resentment in the heart, cursing oneself and others.

blocks.text: 10. Insulting and Slighting Spirits

inline.s: Stepping over wells and stoves, leaping over food and over people; / Destroying children and causing abortion, doing much that is hidden and crooked; / Singing and dancing at the month's end and the year's end, crying out in anger at the new moon and dawn; / Snivelling, spitting, and urinating toward the north, / Humming and wailing before the stove.

Stepping across wells and stoves, leaping over food and over people's bodies. Drowning infants and causing abortions, doing much that is hidden and crooked (conduct that is not upright and aboveboard). Singing and dancing at the dark of the moon (the end of the month) and at the year's end, wailing and raging at the new moon (the start of the month) and at dawn. Facing north to blow the nose, spit, and relieve oneself; facing the stove to sing and weep.

Also lighting incense with stove-fire, cooking food with filthy firewood; / Rising at night naked and bare, carrying out punishments on the eight festivals; / Spitting at shooting stars, pointing at the rainbow; / Often pointing at the Three Luminaries, staring long at sun and moon; / Burning the hills to hunt in spring, cursing fiercely toward the north; / Without cause killing turtles and striking snakes.

Moreover, using stove-fire to light incense and candles, cooking meals with filthy firewood. Rising in the night naked and bare-bodied, carrying out punishments on the eight great solar festivals. Spitting toward shooting stars, pointing a finger at rainbows. Often pointing a finger at the Three Luminaries (sun, moon, and stars), gazing long at the sun and moon. In spring burning the mountain woods to hunt beasts, cursing with foul words toward the north. Without cause killing turtles and striking snakes.

[Carrying out punishments on the eight festivals] The eight festivals are: the beginning of spring, the spring equinox, the beginning of summer, the summer solstice, the beginning of autumn, the autumn equinox, the beginning of winter, and the winter solstice. On the day of a solar term, a person should be pure and peaceful, reflect upon and examine his thoughts, advance in goodness and banish evil, enter into what is right and set aside what is wrong. If punishments are then carried out, it will harm the harmony of Heaven and Earth and diminish the fortune of one's self and family. [Often pointing at the Three Luminaries] The Three Luminaries (sun, moon, and stars) are above; not only do they bestow the grace of shining upon us, but they respond to every prayer. How can one triflingly point a finger at them and thus incur a heavy offense oneself?

blocks.text: Chapter 6: Retribution for Evil

inline.s: For such offenses as these, the Lord of Destinies, according to their gravity, takes away their allotted years; and when the years are used up, they die. If their guilt is more than death can cancel, it then brings calamity upon their descendants.

For those with the offenses described above, the spirit Lord of Destinies, according to the gravity of what they have committed, takes away their span of life; when the span is exhausted, they die. If the debt remains after death, then these unpaid debts of sin bring calamity upon their descendants.

[More guilt than death can cancel] Even by dying to repay one's offenses, one still cannot fully repay them. Here the character “zhai” (obligation) is read as “debt.” “More guilt than death can cancel” is thus the same as “to deserve even more than death.”

Again, for those who seize others' wealth by force, reckoning is made by counting their wives, children, and household members to offset it, gradually reaching death and bereavement. If they do not die, then there come floods, fire, robbers, thieves, the loss of possessions, illness, quarrels, and lawsuits, to offset the value of what they wrongly took.

Again, for those who rely on power and seize people's wealth by force, besides repaying the debt with their own fortune, emolument, and lifespan, the portion that is wanting is borne by their wives and children, gradually extending to death. If they are fortunate enough not to die, then there come the calamities of flood, fire, robbery, theft, the loss of possessions, illness, quarrels, and lawsuits, to repay the value of what they wrongly took.

Again, one who kills people wrongfully is exchanging the sword and the weapon and being killed in turn. One who takes wealth that is not righteous is like eating spoiled dripping meat to relieve hunger or drinking poisoned wine to quench thirst — not that it does not briefly satisfy, but death comes to him as well.

Again, to kill a person wrongfully is like handing the knife to the one killed, that he may hereafter kill you (for one who kills wrongfully is no different from killing himself). One who takes wealth that is not righteous is like eating poisoned dried flesh to appease hunger and drinking poisoned wine to quench thirst — not that it cannot temporarily allay hunger and thirst, but that death follows immediately (not that it does not briefly satisfy, but death comes as well).
[Dripping flesh] “Dried meat” (
fu”
: dried meat, dried fruit. “
Dripping flesh”: meat hung beneath the eaves to dry in the wind; because the dripping of a leaky roof moistens it, it becomes poisonous, and is therefore called “dripping flesh.”

In the Song dynasty there was a Chan master who, when young, had drunk too much wine and, in a quarrel with someone over money, struck him heavily, so that the man fell and died. Fearing punishment he fled, and later, repenting, he left home to become a monk. Practicing hard and diligently, he attained great awakening and became a great Chan master. He would often ascend the seat to teach, with several hundred disciples under him. When he was over seventy, one morning after bathing he ascended the seat and said to the assembly: “Do not move, do not speak — watch this old monk settle a case of forty years ago.”

He sat until noon, when a soldier suddenly arrived at the monastery, bent his bow and set his arrow, ready to kill the master. The old master pressed his palms together and said to the soldier: “The old monk has been waiting here for you for a long time!” The soldier said in astonishment: “I do not know you at all, yet why is it that the moment I see you I want to kill you? Even I myself do not understand the reason.” The old master said: “To repay a debt is fair dealing; please strike, and do not hesitate!” And turning to the assembly he said: “After I die, you should invite this layman to a meal, and after the meal see him on his way. If any of you utters a single word of blame toward him, you will have defied Heaven and betrayed the way of the teacher — you will not be my disciple!” Hearing the master's words, the soldier was all the more perplexed, and insisted that the master make it clear. The master said: “Because you have passed through another life and through reincarnation, you have forgotten! But I am still alive in this world, and so I have not forgotten.” Thereupon he told the soldier what had happened in the past. The soldier, who had never known how to read, suddenly sang out in a loud voice: “Wrong for wrong — when will it ever end? / Life after life enmeshed — is it by chance? / Better to be resolved together with the master, / And now, standing here, go to the Western Paradise.” Having spoken, still holding his bow and arrow, he passed away standing. The master then came down from his seat, shaved his head, gave him a Dharma name, and after changing his clothes placed him in a niche. Then the master himself, sitting cross-legged, took leave of the assembly and passed away in meditation.

blocks.text: Chapter 7: Turning Calamity into Blessing

inline.s: When a good thought arises in the heart, though the good has not yet been done, the auspicious spirit has already followed it. Or when an evil thought arises in the heart, though the evil has not yet been done, the inauspicious spirit has already followed it.

When a thought of good arises in the heart, though the good has not yet been carried out, the auspicious spirit has already followed you, bestowing blessings in many ways. Or when a thought of evil arises in the heart, though the evil has not yet been carried out, the inauspicious spirit has already followed you, sending down calamities in many ways.

Whoever has formerly done evil and afterwards reforms and repents, committing no evil and practicing all good, will in time surely obtain auspicious joy — this is what is meant by turning calamity into blessing.

If one has formerly done evil and afterwards repents and reforms, committing no evil and practicing all good, and persists without ceasing for a long time, then one will surely obtain auspicious joy — this is turning calamity into blessing!

The Great Emperor of Mount Tai taught: “Doing good is like the grass in a spring garden — you do not see it grow, yet it increases each day; doing evil is like the stone that sharpens a knife — you do not see it wear, yet it diminishes each day. Fortune and calamity shift in secret (they move in the dark unperceived), and the deluded do not become aware (they are unable to notice).”

blocks.text: Chapter 8: Practice It Diligently

inline.s: Therefore the auspicious person speaks good, sees good, and does good. Having three goods in a single day, in three years Heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious person speaks evil, sees evil, and does evil. Having three evils in a single day, in three years Heaven will surely send down calamity upon him. Why not strive to practice it?

Therefore, the auspicious person speaks good, sees good, and does good. Having these three goods in a single day (good speech, good seeing, good conduct), in three years Heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious person speaks evil, sees evil, and does evil. Having these three evils in a single day, in three years Heaven will surely send down calamity upon him. Why not strive to practice the three goods (good speech, good seeing, good conduct) so as to gather fortune and dissolve calamity?
[Seeing good] What is contrary to propriety, do not look at;

all things that are crooked and heterodox, killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood, and all manner of disorderly things — look at none of them; look only at the sutras, commentaries, and good books that benefit body and mind.

This chapter sums up the whole work and clearly points out the path of breaking evil and cultivating good: each day practice the three goods (good speech, good seeing, good conduct). The many evils and the many goods are too numerous to recount; to put it concisely, these three — speech, seeing, and conduct — are precisely the practical starting point. Good speech: for example, do not say what is contrary to propriety, delight in speaking of others' goodness, develop the good heart of others, and so on. Good seeing: here “seeing” in fact refers to hearing and seeing; therefore good seeing means, for example, not hearing or seeing what is contrary to propriety, delighting in seeing and hearing good people and good deeds, delighting in reading and listening to good books, constantly seeing one's own faults and not the faults of others, and so on. Good conduct: for example, do not act contrary to propriety, do not tread what is not lawful, be courageous in doing good, at all times do what is convenient for others, in every way perform hidden merit, promoting and guiding in one place and even spreading it to all quarters, transforming the people of the world so that together they practice good. Evil is exactly the opposite of all this.

[In every way performing hidden merit] Whatever one does, one strives to be doing hidden merit. [Hidden merit] Good deeds done in the human world that can be credited in the unseen world. [Hidden virtue] Also called “hidden good (yin zhi
)”, virtue done in secret for others, unknown to anyone.

Before the scripture sets forth the three goods (good speech, good seeing, good conduct), it already says: “When a good thought arises in the heart, though the good has not yet been done, the auspicious spirit has already followed it. Or when an evil thought arises, though the evil has not yet been done, the inauspicious spirit has already followed it.” Therefore a good heart is the root of good speech, good seeing, and good conduct; and good speech, good seeing, and good conduct must spring from the heart to be sincere and reliable. When encountering circumstances and conditions, when dealing with people and handling affairs, one must have a good heart, keeping a compassionate, kind, and serene state of mind. At all times and in all places, examine and reflect on oneself: am I good in heart, good in speech, good in seeing, good in conduct? — night and day, diligently reflect on the four goods.

In the Four Teachings of Liaofan, in the section “The Method of Reforming Faults,” three methods of reforming faults are discussed in detail: reforming in deed, reforming in principle, and reforming in heart. Among them, reforming in heart is the foremost, and the text explains how the three are used in concert. Mr. Liaofan says:

What is called reforming from the heart? Though there be a thousand and ten thousand kinds of faults and evils, they are all created by the mind; if my mind is not enticed by affairs, things, feelings, and circumstances into giving rise to bad thoughts, from where could faults and evils come into being? For a person who cultivates virtue, as to all the various faults and evils such as lust for beauty, the love of fame, the love of wealth, the tendency to anger, and the like, there is no need to seek them out one by one and reform them in principle or in deed one by one; just let this right thought of single-hearted good appear before the mind, and evil thoughts naturally cannot touch it. It is like the sun at high noon, when demons and goblins all flee in disorder — this is the true transmission of refining the one to govern the ten thousand! Faults and evils are created by the mind, and so they must also be reformed from the mind; as in cutting down a poisonous tree, one severs its root directly — why must one cut it off branch by branch and pluck it leaf by leaf?

In sum, the highest method of reforming faults is to govern the mind, keeping the ground of the heart pure at all times and in all places. Because the ground of the heart is pure, as soon as a bad thought stirs — like a stain appearing on snow-white cloth — one immediately becomes aware of it, and upon awareness one at once clears it away. If there are no bad thoughts, naturally there will be no bad words and bad deeds. If the effort of governing the mind is insufficient, and one still cannot achieve that the evil thought “stirs and is at once perceived, and being perceived at once vanishes,” then one must adopt reforming in principle, using reason to drive the faults and evils away, as in the above examples of killing and anger. If reforming in principle also cannot be done, one must adopt reforming in deed: whenever one meets with an affair that would commit a fault or evil, immediately put a stop to it. To use the superior method of the mind's reform while also practicing the lower methods of reform in principle and in deed is the most reliable approach. But if one uses only the lower methods of reform in principle and in deed, without understanding how to use the superior method of the mind's reform — or even does not know to use reform in principle and knows only reform in deed — then to reform faults in this way is not to be wise enough.

For one who already has some skill in contemplating the mind, it is enough to keep the mind of compassion and right mindfulness at all times. If a deluded thought arises, cut it down with a single stroke in that very moment and never let it continue. Great Master Hanshan said: “For a student of the Way, the first thing is to fear birth and death, and the second is to know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is precisely the various kinds of aversion and craving, taking and rejecting, self-conceit, and the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion that appear before you in daily life. Since this is the bitter root of birth and death, once you have resolved to cut it off there is no other technique: simply illuminate it the moment it arises and refuse to let it arise. Where it cannot arise, there it is extinguished; and when it is extinguished, it no longer continues. Using the mind in this way, never letting a single thought slip past, never dimming from thought to thought, your knowing will of itself become keen (you will recognize your own original nature). If the knowing becomes keen (if you recognize your own original nature), then when you meet circumstances the circumstances do not drag the mind along, and when you contemplate the mind the mind does not cling to circumstances; where mind and circumstances do not meet, birth and death have nowhere to lodge. Using the mind in this way, you need not seek anything mysterious elsewhere.” (Mengyou ji, “Instruction to Feng Yanling”)

Mr. Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty used a bottle, black beans, and white beans to practice the work of the mind. Whenever a good thought arose, he would drop a white bean into the bottle; whenever an evil thought arose, he would drop a black bean into the bottle. When he first began, the black beans in the bottle outnumbered the white; afterward they gradually came to be fewer than the white. In the course of time, they were pure white with no black at all. Going one step further, he reached the state where mind and circumstances were both forgotten and he entered the state of ‘not thinking of good, not thinking of evil’; and so in the end he discarded the bottle and the beans and had no further use for them.

blocks.text: 1. Buddha and Mara Are One Mind

inline.s: Recorded from Master Huiming’s Record of Instructions

The good and evil of a person all arise from the mind. When the mind is good, one is a Buddha; when the mind is evil, one is a mara. Buddha and mara have no fixed nature of their own; they shift only according to the good or evil of the thought in the mind.

Honesty, humility, compassion, diligence, and frugality are good thoughts; deceit, arrogance, hatred, lust, and sloth are evil thoughts. Therefore when a single thought is good, the Buddha responds to it, body, mind, and surroundings become peaceful and harmonious, and one is transformed by the Buddha; not only does the good person become better
(not only does one who was already good become more good)
, but the evil person also turns to goodness
(one who was originally evil also turns to goodness)
. When a single thought is evil, the mara responds to it, body, mind, and surroundings turn harsh and vile, and one is transformed by the mara; not only does the evil person become worse
(not only does one who was already evil become more evil)
, but the good person also turns to evil
(one who was originally good also turns to evil)

. Therefore it is said: ordinary being and sage do not go beyond the one mind, good and evil are both made by the mind; when the mind is Buddha, one is Buddha, when the mind is mara, one is mara — such is the principle, surely.

In the age of the Dharma’s end, people are mostly deluded and benighted; good and evil are not distinguished, and they entangle themselves in affliction. There are even those whose hearts are crooked and devious, who deliberately put on good words, thinking that everyone can be deceived
(thinking that everyone can be fooled)
, and that no one in the world is as clever as they
(that everyone in the world is less clever than I)

. Little do they know that vile and evil maras have already gathered about their body and mind; once the power of karma stirs, at the least they meet illness, suffering, loss, and chaos, and at the worst they sink into the evil paths. Even if, relying on past good causes, they escape for a while by luck, yet once the blessings of fortune are exhausted, the evil retribution is without end — is this not perilous! This is the way by which doing good brings down auspiciousness and doing evil brings down calamity, which has held true through all ages and never once failed.

In short, Buddha and mara are not apart from one’s own mind. Why is this? Because all is mind-only. As it is said, when the mind arises, dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, dharmas cease. Yet dharmas have no self-nature, and dharmas are neither deviant nor correct. When the mind is correct and one practices a deviant dharma, the deviant dharma becomes correct; when the mind is deviant and one practices a correct dharma, the correct dharma becomes deviant. When the mind is good, one transforms mara into Buddha; when the mind is evil, one transforms Buddha into mara. At the very moment we raise a thought and stir a mind, may we not be careful!

blocks.text: 2. Song of the Good Person

inline.s: Lü Xinwu
Original note: the Master
(Lü Xinwu)
was named Kun, courtesy name Shujian, a native of Ningling, a presented scholar of the Jiajing era of the Ming, who rose in office to Junior Minister of Justice
(rose in office to Vice Minister of Justice)

Hongmou’s note: everyone knows to love and admire a good person, yet in one’s intentions and conduct there are times when one comes close to being not good! Here they are listed one by one — who is a good person, who is not a good person — and one may see it in each matter as it arises. Those with resolve may examine themselves by it.

Translation: everyone knows to love and admire a good person, yet in one’s own intentions and conduct there are times when one comes close to being not good! Now the Song of the Good Person sets out one by one what a good person is and what a not-good person is. How one is a good person and how one is a not-good person may be seen quite plainly from the various matters spoken of in the song. Those who have the resolve to be good persons may use it to examine themselves.
Heaven and earth give birth to all things, yet none is more precious than the human being. Among human beings there are good persons, who rise still higher above the human kind.
[Among human beings there are good persons, who rise still higher above the human kind] A good person among human beings is again one who stands out above the rest of humankind.
The good person puts loyalty and trust first; the good person prizes filial piety and fraternal love. The good person knows shame and honor; the good person keeps rite and righteousness.

[Filial piety and fraternal love] also written “filial piety and fraternal duty”: to be filial to father and mother and to love and respect one’s elder brothers. [Fraternal love, tì] to love and respect one’s elder brother.
The good person does not indulge in wine; the good person does not dote on courtesans. The good person does not gamble for money; the good person does not give way to temper.
[Giving way to temper] to act on hot-headed impulse.
The good person does not rely on wealth; the good person does not lean on power. The good person does not default on grain tax; the good person does not encroach on land.

[Not defaulting on grain tax] not owing the grain tax paid to the government. [Government grain] in former times, the tax grain paid to the government office. [Not encroaching on land] not seizing and occupying the fields of others.
The good person does not instigate; the good person does not envy. The good person does not tell lies; the good person does not mock and tease.
[Instigate] to egg on and direct (others to do evil). [Mock and tease (xuè)] to make fun of and play tricks on.
The good person has no idle talk; the good person does not slander and criticize. The good person has no bad friends; the good person has no dissolute gatherings.
[Idle talk] also written “divisive talk”: words that estrange others. [Bad friends] wicked companions. [Dissolute gatherings] debauched parties.
The good person is not rustic and rough; the good person is not wild and perverse. The good person is not lazy and indolent; the good person does not squander and waste.
[Rustic and rough] crude and reckless. [Wild and perverse (bèi)] frenzied and contrary to reason. [Squander and waste] to spend lavishly and wastefully.
The good person is not frivolous; the good person is not ostentatious. The good person is not slovenly; the good person is not bizarre.
[Bizarre (qiāo xī)] crafty and strange.
The good person is not overbearing; the good person is not benighted. The good person saves others from trouble and calamity; the good person bestows kindness and benefit.
[Overbearing] tyrannical and violent. [Benighted] muddled and foolish.
The good person grants convenience; the good person yields the advantage. The evil person curses the good person; the good person does not answer back.
The evil person strikes the good person; the good person only avoids him. Be the other great or small, the good person gives no offense.
Be the matter great or small, the good person accords with heavenly principle. The rich person who is good, his hidden merit reaches later generations.
[Hidden merit] good deeds done in this world that may be credited in the netherworld. [Hidden merit reaches later generations] the blessing of hidden merit benefits the people of later generations.
The noble person who is good, his countryfolk do not curse him. The poor person who is good — what of a thousand qing of land?

[Countryfolk] fellow villagers. [Curse (lì)] to revile. [The poor person who is good — what of a thousand qing of land] the benefit of a poor person’s being good far surpasses the possession of a thousand qing of land.
The lowly person who is good counts for more than princes and nobles. The young person who is good, his virtue and renown equal his elders’.
[The lowly person who is good counts for more than princes and nobles] the lowly person who is good is far more honored than princes and nobles.
The aged person who is good covers over the offenses of a whole life. The weak man who is good makes the strong man ashamed of himself.
The evil person who is good, his fame weighs a thousand times more. The good person is a village’s treasure; the good person is a family’s and a nation’s auspice.
[The good person is a family’s and a nation’s auspice] the good person is the auspicious omen (a sign of good fortune) of a family and a nation.
The good person moves gods and spirits; the good person touches heaven and earth. He is not a human being made in vain; he speaks out a breath of air on heaven’s behalf.

[The good person moves gods and spirits; the good person touches heaven and earth] the good person moves gods and spirits, the good person moves heaven and earth. [Speaks out a breath of air on heaven’s behalf] heavenly principle is often misunderstood and defiled by people, and the good person, making himself the example, confirms heavenly principle, clarifies heavenly principle, and spreads heavenly principle.
Alas! A hundred years once gone never return; do not be an evil person and sully the world.
[Sully the world] to defile the world. [Sully (wò)] to stain, to make dirty.

blocks.text: 3. The Ledger of Merit and Demerit

inline.s: Translated and annotated by Mingde

The Ledger of Merit and Demerit is a register by which those who refrain from evil and practice good spur themselves and examine themselves self-critically. It has two parts, the merit grid (good deeds) and the demerit grid (evil deeds), one page a month, bound into a book. Day by day one records the merit or demerit of one’s behavior as good or evil, such as one merit, ten merits, a hundred merits, one demerit, ten demerits, a hundred demerits. Only the number is recorded, not the deed, and it is entered separately into the merit grid or the demerit grid. Each evening one settles the account; merit and demerit are offset against each other, and the remainder is the fixed merit or the fixed demerit. For example, if today one has ten merits and one demerit, then today’s fixed merit is nine; if it is ten demerits and one merit, then today’s fixed demerit is nine. Doing thus every day, at the end of the month one makes a small tally, accumulating the number of merits and demerits of the month, then offsets merit against demerit and carries the resulting merits or demerits over to the following month. At the end of the year, one again carries over the accumulated merits or demerits into the following year. Proceeding thus, one keeps clear measure in mind day by day, month by month, year by year, and practices diligently without ceasing.

In one day one is sure to have more than ten merits to be cultivated; when accumulated to half a month, then over and above the merits of one’s own grade one enters an additional ten merits; this prizes pure goodness. If in the midst there are one or two matters that do not meet the standard, then none may be entered separately. When urging one’s own kin to goodness, a single great matter counts as ten merits; when it concerns an outsider it counts as only one merit — this honors kin and exalts filial piety and fraternal love. Ten merits in a day, and ten more entered at the half month, means a month may reach three hundred and twenty merits and a year four thousand merits. Such merit is extremely easy to accumulate and the recompense extremely swift. Yet one must be strict in self-reproach: even the most trivial demerit must be recorded, and one must not gloss over demerits while keeping full count of merits. All the accumulated merits are matters of daily, ordinary conduct that need no money, therefore poor men and women may all practice it. As for great perversity, wicked rebellion, killing, theft, the destruction of relationships, and a woman’s wantonness and violence, her cruel slaughter of other living beings, and her jealousy that cuts off progeny — these are grave sins and extreme evils, and are not within the demerit limit. All within the grid are everyday household matters; as for great loyalty and great filial piety, great integrity and great righteousness, and the official who so benefits the people that a single deed may stand for ten thousand good acts — these likewise are not within the merit limit.

The idiom “bending the chimney and moving the firewood” is exactly “to rescue before it occurs.” [Bending the chimney and moving the firewood] A guest, seeing that the chimney of the master’s stove was straight and that firewood was piled beside it, said to the master: “You should rebuild a bent chimney, lest the sparks keep flying out, and move the firewood to a distance. Otherwise, a fire might break out.” The master fell silent and did not answer. Before long the house indeed caught fire, and the neighbors came together to fight the blaze, and fortunately they put it out. Then the master slaughtered an ox and set out wine to thank his neighbors. Those burned in the fire (their heads scalded and faces blistered) were seated in the places of honor, and the rest were seated in order by the size of their contribution, but the guest who had advised him to “bend the chimney and move the firewood” was not invited. Then someone said to the master: “If back then you had listened to the guest’s advice, you would not have suffered the fire, nor would you have gone to the expense of laying out a feast. Now when you appraise the merit and invite the guests, why is the one who advised ‘bending the chimney and moving the firewood’ not invited, while those who were burned are honored as the guests of honor?” Only then did the master awaken, and he hurried to invite that guest. In one day, reverently serving the spirits and ancestors, or praying for the blessings of one’s parents, seeking good conditions, and with utmost sincerity observing the fasts.
one merit
Repairing and setting up temples and sacred images, offering to the Buddha and feeding the monks.
one merit per hundred coins
Gathering written paper and burning it.
one merit per hundred characters
Constantly thinking of the sages, worthies, immortals, and Buddhas, keeping them solemnly in the mind, up to fifteen days.
ten merits

Up to awakening and sleeping with spiritual penetration, the luminous jewel-like appearance constantly flowing through the heart and lungs, as if wandering in the heavenly palace or hearing the speech of the gods. Expounding the teachings of the worthies and sages.
a hundred merits each
Profaning the scriptures. Making dirty written paper. Discharging
(urine and feces)
and spitting without regard to the three lights
(sun, moon, and stars)
. Praying for blessings and warding off calamity, yet not practicing good deeds, and vowing evil wishes with sacrificial animals. A woman fond of entering temples.
one demerit each
Mocking, insulting, and slandering the sages and worthies. Disrespecting the ancestors
ten demerits each
Striking and cursing the gods and spirits. Defiling temples. Advocating rebellion against the sages.
a hundred demerits each

[Gathering written paper and burning it] In ancient times, all paper bearing writing carried the words of the sages, so it had to be respected; it must not be defiled or discarded, but should be reverently burned. blocks.text: 11. The Grid of Preserving the Mind

inline.s: To forget one’s good deeds and to be free of self is placed first.
[Forgetting one’s good deeds] not to store up the good one has done within the mind.
[Forgetting one’s good deeds and being free of self]

The Record of the Four Lessons of Master Liaofan says: to use wealth to help people, without within seeing oneself, without without seeing the recipient, and in the middle not seeing the wealth given — this is the emptiness of the three wheels, this is single-minded purity. Doing thus, one dou of grain can plant immeasurable blessings, and a single coin can eradicate the offenses of a thousand kalpas. [The emptiness of the three wheels] the “three wheels” are the giver, the recipient, and the thing given; after giving, not keeping these three wheels in the mind is called “the emptiness of the three wheels.”
In the course of a single day, if one’s words and deeds are all good, and one’s mind is set on aiding the world and guiding the multitude,
one merit
and if for fifteen days one shares goodness with others and mends one’s faults day by day,
ten merits
and if for a whole month no selfish thought appears, one’s thoughts are few and dreams cease, and one’s intent grows ever more sincere,
a hundred merits
and if one is constantly thus, compassion
(utterly sincere)
natural, holding to an empty, rounded responsiveness
(the mind, without clinging, treating people and matters with fullness)
counts as immeasurable merit
Lustful thoughts, greedy thoughts, evil thoughts, envious thoughts, thoughts of flattering the world, turning here and there
(tossing about)
are not removed.
one demerit
If evil thoughts turn and linger for several days and show themselves in one’s actions
ten demerits

[Sharing goodness with others] When doing good, inviting others to join in. It also means: when one has a virtue, being willing that others be like oneself; when others have a strength, learning from them. [With no private thought appearing, few thoughts and dreams at rest, kindness ever more sincere] Private thoughts and scattered notions do not arise, one thinks little and dreams cease, and one's intent grows ever more sincere. Kun
kǔn
: utterly sincere. [Turning over and over] Tossing and turning, unable to be still.

Not going out the door, yet saving ten thousand lives."

Spending no wealth, yet performing ten thousand merits."

(Filiality and friendship, skillful means, can be done on the spot; bearing insult with a patient heart, the merit is boundless. This is what is meant by "spending no wealth, yet performing ten thousand merits.")
Resorting to no laws, yet ferrying ten thousand people."
(Praising good people, rejoicing in good deeds, printing and publishing good books, arousing good thoughts. This is what is meant by "resorting to no laws, yet ferrying ten thousand people.")
